LA SALLE CADETS INSPECTION-RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO ACCESS BY CENTRAL WALK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege that concerns every member of the house.
Last summer, while this house was in session, the La Salle cadets paraded on the lawns in front of these parliament buildings. Later, during the evening, several members of parliament-if I am correctly informed, members representing all the major parties-entered the front gate and attempted to proceed to the House of Commons by the main walk, and were stopped from doing so by a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They explained to him that they were members of parliament. That made no difference. An order had been issued that everyone must come to the House of Commons around by the east block. Therefore these members had to proceed to the House of Commons via the east block.
I wish at this time, Mr. Speaker, to protest strongly against the placing of members of this house in such a position that they must approach the building after the fashion of the butcher boy delivering a pound of sausage by the tradesmen's entrance.
Last Friday evening the La Salle cadets were parading again on the lawns in front of the House of Commons. I had occasion to approach the house by the central walk, and, when about half way between the front gate and the House of Commons, I was informed that the La Salle cadets were being paraded and reviewed, and that they were being reviewed by a special visitor from Rome, Italy, Brother Athanase Emile. Knowing of the record of the La Salle cadets, and being interested in this distinguished clerical visitor, I stopped about half way between the front gate and the House of Commons and watched the cadets being inspected by the visitor, followed by Colonel Purves of national defence headquarters, a member of the Canadian armoured corps. I saw these cadets very smartly give the general salute to the distinguished clerical visitor.
At that time a staff sergeant of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police approached me and informed me that the grounds for that period were reserved for the La Salle cadets, the officers of the Department of National Defence on the grounds, and the distinguished visitor, and that I would have to move.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am one of those to whom on such occasions the scroll of British history swiftly unfolds itself before mine eyes, and I am quickly moved by such events. Therefore I informed the staff sergeant that I was a member of parliament and as such I did not intend to budge, come what may. At this point the staff sergeant was most courteous, I might say almost embarrassed. He explained to me the reason for the grounds being reserved. I protested and said that this was a violation of the rights of members of the House of Commons, and no explanation from him could alter my determination to stand my ground, since I considered this order an indignity upon members of the House of Commons.
In view of the fact that the zephyrs of indignity can soon become the winds of intolerance, and the winds of intolerance the hurricane of tyranny, I wish to protest most vigorously against this transgression of the freedom of members within the precincts of the House of Commons, and against this indignity to members of parliament, to the representatives of the people, and thus indirectly to the Canadian people as a whole.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: JUDGE OF EXCHEQUER COURT TO BE CHIEF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
On May 26, I gave this house a statement of the legislation which remained to be dealt with during the present session. At that time I indicated that amendments to the Judges Act and to the Railway Act relating to the board of transport commissioners would be introduced.
The proposed legislation has reference to government plans for a reconstitution of the board of transport commissioners in view of substantially increased responsibilities which it is expected that board will have to assume over the coming years. I am now in a position to give further details regarding the proposed legislation.
A single bill will be introduced to amend the Railway Act, the Exchequer Court Act and the

Judges Act, 1946. This bill will provide that a judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada shall hold the office of chief commissioner of the board of transport commissioners. Such judge, however, while acting as chief commissioner, will devote his full time to the work of the board.
The bill will also provide, with a consequential amendment in the Judges Act of 1946, that in the light of the foregoing change the exchequer court will be increased by one, to consist thereafter of the president and four judges, instead of the president and three judges as at present.
The bill will not in any way change the term of appointment to the post of chief commissioner from a. ten-year period. When a judge of the exchequer court has served for this term as chief commissioner he will, unless his term of office is extended, return to the exchequer court; his successor will then be appointed from that body.
Colonel J. A. Cross, C.M.G., D.S.O., K.C., whose term of office expires in February, 1950, having been advised of the intention of the government to reconstitute the board as indicated and of the heavy additional duties and responsibilities which the board will be expected to perform over the coming years, has informed me that, in the circumstances, taking into consideration the fact that he is not far from completing his term of office as chairman, it would be in the best interests of all concerned for the government to make immediate arrangements for a new appointment to the post of chief commissioner and has accenting ly tendered his resignation as chief commissioner of the board, to take effect at the pleasure of the government.
The government shares the view expressed by Colonel Cross, and intends to accept his resignation, as soon as the bill I have referred to is enacted. I am pleased to be able to announce that the Hon. Maynard Brown Archibald, a member of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, has agreed, when the necessary legislation has been passed, to accept the appointment of chief commissioner of the board1 of transport commissioners. Mr. Justice Archibald will then be first appointed to the Exchequer Court of Canada and immediately thereafter be named as chief commissioner of the board.
I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to extend to Colonel Cross the thanks of the government for the valuable services performed by him during the years he has been holding the very responsible position of chief commissioner of the board of transport commissioners. A former attorney general of the province of Saskatchewan,

Colonel Cross brought with him to Ottawa years of experience at the bar which have been of great service to him in his capacity of chief commissioner, and which, in turn, have enabled him to perform many years of devoted public service to Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: S. S. "ABEGWEIT" INQUIRY AS TO STRUCTURAL CHANGES
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Has any decision been made concerning the planking of the railway car deck of Q.S.M.V. Abegweit to permit trucks to drive on and off that deck under their own power?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: S. S. "ABEGWEIT" INQUIRY AS TO STRUCTURAL CHANGES
speechtext:
Yes, a decision has been arrived at. For some time consideration has been given to the planking of the lower deck of the Abegweit. After weighing all the arguments for and against, the government has decided that a steel floor over the entire deck should be laid at the earliest possible opportunity. At the present time the Abegweit is in dry dock in Montreal, and should be ready to proceed to Northumberland strait on the tenth of this month. Before the necessary steel becomes available and is installed, a period of seven or eight weeks would elapse, which is far too long a time to immobilize a vessel costing upwards of $7,000,000. Furthermore, the Abegweit will be needed shortly to take care of the tourist traffic to Prince Edward Island.
As an alternative, it has been decided to cover half the lower deck with wooden planks specially treated with fire-resistant paint. Instructions were given to make a start on this work yesterday, and I am advised that to complete this job wall require twelve days at the most. The Abegweit would, therefore, be ready to proceed to Borden at the latest on the twentieth of this month, in sufficient time to take care of the heavy summer traffic.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before the motion for third reading is put, Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a brief amendment. It relates to a provision that was introduced into this legislation last Wednesday evening, June 2. Prior to that time the only announcement that had been made with respect to the suspension of certain British preferential tariffs from May 19, 1949 to June 30. 1949, was to the effect that these tariffs would definitely be off for that period of time. However, last Wednesday evening the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in what I felt to be only a plausible defence of his action, announced that the government had decided to introduce a proviso. That proviso took the form of an amendment to the resolution which was before the house, and it is now in the bill before us. The proviso suggested by the government would give to the governor in council the power to suspend any of those suspensions during the period in question. If I may get away from the use of the double negative which is inevitable in discussing this matter, it amounts to this. Tariffs on certain British goods are now off, and will be off until June 30, 1949. But this new clause, which has been put in, gives the government power by order in council to put any or all of those tariffs, which have thus been taken off, back on during that period.
I have two strenuous objections to this clause. In the first place, we of this group regarded the action of the government in taking off these tariffs as good, as the proverbial step in the right direction. Now that this step has been taken we do not like the idea of a few doors and windows being left open for some of these tariffs to be reimposed. I am sure those on the government side, such as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) and the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch), who voted with us when we tried to strike this clause out of the legislation during the resolution stage, will share our view that the removal of certain tariffs on British goods was a step in the right direction and should stand.
But in addition to my own support of the proposal to remove these tariffs, I strongly object to the government asking parliament to give it yet another power to take action by
Customs Tariff

order in council. I know the government has multitudinous powers by order in council now. I know the very bill which is before us has in other respects powers given to the government to make changes by order in council. But that does not justify giving yet another such power.
I was most interested in the support given my suggestion the other night by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) and others of the group to my right. They took the view that whatever their stand was on the tariff question, they simply could not support this further addition to the order in council powers of the present government; and I was impressed by the way in which a number of my hon. friends to the right took that stand and stood up to be counted with us when the vote was taken in committee.
In fact it would seem that the issue is quite clear. It is not only the issue of the tariff question itself; there is this overriding issue of the request of the government for this additional power to take action by order in council. The other evening when I moved a subamendment to strike out this power, at the resolution stage, I noted that the Minister of Finance said he welcomed the subamendment and was quite prepared to leave it to the house to make a decision. I wondered whether the members of his own party caught the full import of his statement that he would leave it to the house. I thought he was making it clear that the government was not going to stand or fall by his proposal; that in effect it was a free vote, and I thought that many Liberals would vote in a liberal manner when the vote was called. Today, when I move the same amendment at this third reading stage, I hope a free vote will be offered, and that the government will permit the house to decide on this important question.
The reasons given by the minister the other evening for introducing this order in council power related to what he described as uncertain conditions in the world and particularly in world trade at the present time. As I say, that defence struck me as only plausible; for we have all been conscious of the fact that there are in Canada certain interests which did not welcome the removal of these British preferential tariffs for even the short period of thirteen and a half months. We are conscious of the fact that strong recommendations have been made to the government to reimpose all or at least some of these tariffs immediately. Frankly, I do not think the government should leave itself open to the temptation to yield to those representations, by having in this legislation

the power by order in council to put any or all these tariffs on once more.
There is the situation, Mr. Speaker. It is not necessary for me to take any more of the time of the house in presenting it. I hope the Minister of Finance will again say that it is up to the house to decide. I hope my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party, led by the hon. member for Stanstead, the hon. member for Nanaimo and others who voted for us the other evening, will succeed in persuading others of their number today to vote with us against this wide order in council power. I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Winnipeg South will be joined today by other Liberals who will vote against this open door and these open windows which would make possible the reimposition of tariffs on British goods during the period of time between now and June 30, 1949.
To bring the matter to a head, Mr. Speaker, I have pleasure in moving, seconded by my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis):
That Bill No. 333 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of amending section 4 thereof by deleting subsection (c), namely lines 26, 27 and 28 on page 7 of the bill.
If I may read those three lines, they are as follows:
_ (c) The governor in council may at any time withdraw, in whole or in part, the suspensions in duty provided for in paragraphs (a) and (b).
The effect of my amendment would be to delete that subparagraph from the bill.

I should like to make one point before this amendment is voted upon. We are now well into the middle of June. It will be at least the end of June, I presume, before we leave here, and in the ordinary course of events we shall be back in a little more than six months. There will be only a short period during which parliament will not be in session. I cannot believe that for the sake of this short period it is necessary to contravene a principle which has been so stoutly maintained here in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have just a word in reply to what has been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
This amendment, of course, is the amendment the hon. member moved wThen we were in committee. Since he has stated his reasons for supporting the amendment, however, I think I should state why the proposed section is contained in the bill.

As I informed the house when the budget resolutions were brought down, suspension of the tariffs on cotton and rayon goods was primarily for the purpose of giving some price relief to the Canadian consumer and assuring adequate supplies of needed textiles. Before taking that action I received assurances from the representatives of the British government, the board of trade, that, in the event of the duty being removed, advantage would not be taken of that by British exporters, to add the amount of the duty to the price. I can see no particular reason for giving the British exporter the benefit of the removal of such duties. I have no doubt that the assurances which I received will be lived up to, but I do not want to give away all my ammunition until I am sure that they have been. The removal of the duty is not to benefit anyone outside this country; it is to benefit people inside the country.
The second point I wish to make is this. Because of the provisional application of the Geneva agreements, we are obliged to extend this removal or suspension of duties to a very large number of other countries-mostfavoured-nation countries-which include the majority of the trading countries of the world. I have not received any such assurance from those countries, and it is pretty difficult for me to say what conditions might develop there.
For these reasons it seems prudent to take power, as is done in the bill, to withdraw this suspension if conditions do not work out as we believe they will. As I said when the bill was in committee stage, I do not consider this is a great or vital issue on which the government need stand or fall. All hon. members are free to vote on it as they wish. Personally I shall vote against the amendment, as I did when it was proposed in committee, for the reasons which I have mentioned. I believe it is prudent good business to maintain this reserve.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put there is a statement the minister has just made which I think should be clarified. He said that owing to the provisional application of Geneva agreements the government was bound, or felt itself bound, to extend to all other countries the tariff treatment given to Great Britain under this bill.

speechtext: The most-favoured-nation countries.

To the most-favoured-nation countries, and to the seventeen countries which have signed the provisional agreement. My 5849-3104
Customs Tariff
understanding is that although we have provisionally applied the tariff changes agreed to at Geneva, we have not yet applied the agreement. We have not yet agreed to it, and therefore we are not bound, if we make further tariff changes now in favour of certain countries, to apply those changes to all other countries.
With respect I say to the minister that he is slightly confused. I do not think his argument applies to this tariff adjustment. It seems to me the only country with which we have to deal in this respect is Great Britain. If he has had the assurance from that country which he says he had, then surely we can take their word at its face value and believe that they will not take advantage of this adjustment by changing their prices to undersell us. I do not think the minister has advanced any good reason why the amendment should not be accepted.

Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to revise and consolidate the law respecting the levying of income tax and the administration thereof.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the formal resolution to precede the introduction of what was known last year as Bill No. 454, to revise and consolidate the income tax law.
I would hope	that	the	resolution might	beadopted with,	shall	I	say, a	minimum	ofdiscussion in	order	that the	bill may	be
introduced and distributed to members.
It is a technical and complicated and very lengthy bill.	A great	many	changes have
been made since the original bill was introduced last year, following representations received from groups throughout the country, boards of trade, the bar association, the chartered accountants association, and so on, and also as a result of further study by our own staffs. It would be my intention, as I indicated a short time ago, to refer the bill to the banking and commerce committee for detailed study after it receives second reading. I think the bill could be more effectively dealt with there, where taxation experts and the draftsmen could appear and explain the various provisions. A tremendous amount of work has been done on the bill since it was introduced almost a year ago, and I believe it represents a forward step in the revision and consolidation of our income tax law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there any change in tax rates or exemptions, or are the changes with respect to administration only?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are no such changes as my hon. friend mentions. Appropriate amendments were made to the Income War Tax Act, which was passed yesterday, with respect to any changes of policy included in the bill. There is nothing in the bill which changes tax rates or exemptions or anything of the sort. It is simply a revision and consolidation, with certain policy changes with respect to administrative detail rather than income tax rates.
As I indicated in my budget speech, the bill will not be given retroactive effect but will become effective from the first of January next, that is for the next calendar year. As the committee will appreciate, that will afford
Income Tax Act
opportunity for further changes at the next session of parliament should others be found necessary between now and then.

This bill is lengthy and will require a great deal of consideration. If the minister hopes to get it through the house this session, I suggest that the banking and commerce committee sit as often as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am in the hands of this committee, but if it could be arranged, I would like to have the banking and commerce committee take up the bill early next week and work on it steadily. Many sections wall not be controversial, and will simply interest lawyers. The heart of the bill is contained in fifteen or twenty sections, which will require particular attention. They deal with such things as the rules for depreciation and valuation of inventories. They are very important from the point of view of the amount of tax collected, and will require careful consideration by the committee.
The provisions of the bill have already received much study by such representative bodies as boards of trade, the chartered accountants association, the bar association, and others with specialized knowledge. I think the committee will find that the officials who have, worked long and hard on the bill will be in a position to explain it thoroughly before the committee. I would hope that we could get it through this year, and I think we should make every effort to do so.

I have one comment to make. Ever since parliament assembled in the autumn of 1945 we have had this bill dangled before our eyes, and the Minister of Finance the first time said he hoped to introduce it the next year. We all know what the task has been. There is no use crying over spilt milk, but it is most unfortunate that it comes down almost within a fortnight of the time we are told the house will adjourn. I appreciate the work that has been done, the fact that various competent people have been consulted with regard to the bill, and that there will be a great deal of expert evidence available. Nevertheless the responsibility will rest with this house, and I feel that to ask the house, in the short time available, to do the job that should be done, is to propose what is almost impossible. It is in the highest degree unfortunate that it was not brought before us many weeks ago.

I want to ask the minister one question, the purpose of which is to help me in something that I should do by telegram. Are there any changes with respect
to depletion in coal mines? I ask that ques-

tion because certain people in the coal mining industry in Alberta are anxious to appear before the committee. This is Tuesday, and I should like to let them know whether they should come or just stay at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no change in the bill in its present form so far as matters of policy' are concerned. As I said in answer to the leader of the opposition, the job of this

bill is not primarily to change existing tax policy. It is to consolidate, simplify and improve the arrangement of the bill rather than to make a wholesale revision of the taxing provisions. Any' change that is to be made with respect to taxation of co-operatives or any other enterprise in this country should be made here in the house as a matter of budget presentation and not in a revision of a bill of this kind. I would not undertake to do that.

The minister says he is in a great hurry to get this bill before the banking and commerce committee, and he would like to have it put through the house at this session if possible. On the other hand he tells us that the committee will have no power to make any changes whatever in the bill. The bill is merely going to the committee so as to give experts an opportunity of explaining it to the lawy'ers and those who may be administering it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say' they would not have power to make changes in the bill.
I understood the minister to say that a few moments ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No committee of this house can change taxation provisions, but it may' change administrative provisions.

And that does not change anything. The taxes remain the same. The co-operatives are still taxed, and the depletion allowance for coal mines is not changed. Nothing is changed, but the mechanics are simplified for those who will administer the bill. It must be a pretty complicated bill. My object in rising is simply to make this point. If we are not going to change any'-thing in the banking and commerce committee, so far as policy is concerned, why waste time sending it to the committee? Why should we not go to work on it right here where we may make changes, and after we have studied the basic laws contained in the bill, then, if it is desired to send it to another committee to have the mechanics clarified, that can be done. Would that not be the quicker way of doing it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had thought of that. There are two alternatives-to have it considered in committee of the whole or to refer it to the banking and commerce committee. The banking and commerce committee can make any' amendments that we can make in committee of the whole. There is no difference so far as amendments are concerned. The banking and commerce committee would be free to recommend amendments just as the com-

mittee here can; but my main purpose in sending it to the banking and commerce committee was to enable interested members to get explanations of the various sections direct from the tax officials of my department and officers of the ministry of justice, rather than having the information relaj'ed through me in the house. It seemed to me to be the more efficient way of dealing with this rather technical bill-because it is technical. Any income tax statute, I do not care in what country, where there is a system of progressive income tax, is bound to be complicated, and the reason it is complicated is that you try to allow for deductions and exemptions and all that sort of thing so that the tax will be in relation to ability to pay. \ou could make a very simple income tax law if you did not have exemptions and deductions for medical expenses, depletion, depreciation and all these other things, which are intended to make the law more equitable. That is why it is complicated. I speak whereof I know because I have had occasion in the practice of my profession to look these acts over, and I really think that the work of considering this consolidation and revision, which was intended to be primarily a simplifying job, to make it more easily understood and applied by the general public, could be better undertaken in the banking and commerce committee than in the house. I have no objection, but I really think that it would be better if we sent it to the banking and commerce committee.

I am not going to argue the point with the minister. He has not convinced me that it would not be more expeditious to deal with it in committee here, the only place where we can change the basic setup. However, I wish to ask him a question in connection with the depletion allowance for coal mines. I have had something to do with that. Large corporations across the country get hold of leases-the Hudson's Bay company in the west, Dosco in the east. Canadian Collieries in British Columbia-and they have large coal deposits which they do not. operate. They sublease the coal to a small operator who then invests the capital and carries on the operation, but the large concern, which has nothing to do with the development, is allowed that ten-cent depletion on each ton of coal. I have made representations to the finance department during the war and at other times on that very point. We are trying to have that situation changed so that the actual operator should get this allowance, not the lessor or the man who leases or subleases that section of his mining set-up to a smaller operator. It is completely unfair and unjust that the lessor should get the depletion
Income Tax Act
allowance; it should go to the one who is actually carrying on the operation. Has the minister given any thought to the matter? He was not in that department at the time. The present Minister of Justice was -then Minister of Finance. But we did not get anywhere with the suggestion. It should be given some thought.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not too familiar with the manner in which depletion is handled. I know that for a great many years a certain allowance has been paid out for depletion of coal mines. It now falls primarily within the jurisdiction of the Department of National Revenue, although policy matters of course would be settled in the Department of Finance. No doubt I shall be more familiar with it before the bill gets through the committee.

I think we are all glad to see some codification of the Income Tax Act of 1917 and subsequent amendments. Would any serious inconvenience or embarrassment be caused to the country or the taxpayers generally if we left this bill over until the next session of parliament? We are about to have three sittings a day, starting this Wednesday. The estimates are going through, and some of us would like to pay a little attention to them on behalf of our constituents. Other committees are still sitting, including the prices committee, the personnel of which includes members who would be interested in this bill, and they cannot- be in two places at the same time. I believe we could go into the bill much more thoroughly and get a much better idea of its complicated technical provisions if the minister would put it over until the next session, unless there are strong and pertinent reasons why we should deal with it now.
We have had the bill in its original form before us for some time-sufficient time, I might say. But briefs have been received by the government from a great many associations, and some of their ideas have been incorporated in the bill which shortly we are to see for the first time. If that revised bill had been brought down a month or so ago. we might have been able to do some ground work on the revisions. But the government has not seen fit to do that. I think wre should enter more than a mild protest against the government's listening to representations of those who are not representatives of the people at all, accepting their suggestions where they proved to be acceptable, incorporating then, in the measure and then flashing the bill on the house in the last two weeks of the session. I think that is unfair. The bill should be given a hoist until the next session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not pressing it. I think it is desirable that we get this bill on the statute book. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has chided me for delay. The hon. member for Rosedale has just said that we ought to have brought this bill down a month earlier. I want to remind the committee that there are only twenty-four hours in a day; that applies to me and perhaps even more so to the members of my staff. Work has been going on in connection with this bill day after day and month after month. I myself have had meeting after meeting, interlarded between budget meetings, to go over the provisions of the bill. I can assure my hon. friend, who has never practised law but who, I know, is trained in law, that it is a long and tedious business. It was not possible to bring this bill in earlier. I am not suggesting at all that we should force the bill through at this session, but I think it is possible to put it through. Just about as many calls are made on my time as on the time of most members of the house, but I intend to try to devote a good deal of time to attendance at meetings of the banking and commerce committee when the bill is under consideration.
If it proves unwise or undesirable to try to pass the bill this session, of course, as I say, we will not force it through. But I think we ought to make a start. If we do not make a start on these things, we never finish them. The bill has alreadj' been put over for a year. I brought it in last session so that its main provisions could be studied during the year. Study has been given to the bill, and I think it is in fairly good shape now. I should like to see it. considered in detail by the banking and commerce committee. I should like to see it made effective as of January 1, 1949. People will know what the law is to be from that time on. If it is not possible to do that, well and good. But I think we ought to buckle down and try to get it through.

I agree with the minister in one thing, namely, that this bill should go to the banking and commerce committee. That seems to me to be the most sensible idea. I agree wholly with most of what the hon. member for Rosedale said, with this exception. I cannot quite follow him when he suggests that- the bill be held over. However, I most fully agree with him on what is happening now.
I realize how busy the minister has been.
I know he has not been idling. Nevertheless the fact is that we are almost in the dying days of the session, and this bill, which has

been foreshadowed for three years, and which last year was brought forward with the idea that this year we would have plenty of time to consider it, is brought dow'n at this moment. \Y hat does that mean? I do not want to press the point, but if this bill goes through, it really means that we have just rubber-stamped it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course not. I will answer that now.

That is not as it should be. What really happens is that the minister's officials-and I have great respect for them-are going to give us a synopsis of what other people have said, and we shall have to take it. I know they are competent; nevertheless we shall have to take all this at second hand. The minister says the committee cannot take evidence. I suppose if consideration of the bill is to be completed within the next three weeks, it is almost physically impossible that much evidence should be heard. As has already been pointed out, with all the multitudinous duties that press in on us in these last few weeks, it is almost physically impossible to give it the necessary time. It is like crying over spilt milk, but it is just another case of the house being an automatic rubber stamp for the will of the government; and that is not wise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that there is no rubber-stamping about this at all. There is nothing really new in this bill. It has been primarily a drafting job by experts. I do not want to offend any hon. member of the committee, but let me say that only a relatively small number of members here, by training or experience, are competent to give this bill analysis. That is the truth. The ones who are competent to give it that critical analysis might go over the hundred odd sections, of which perhaps fifteen or twenty are really vital, and do it in a relatively short time. But the hard job in connection with this bill has been to weigh the various arguments.
That is what we should do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We should, yes. But a great deal of it is so specialized that, with deference to every member of the committee, the consideration which they can give, let us say, to the specialized clauses relating to depreciation and depletion may be questionable. Some can be helpful, of course; others are not at all interested. There is no particularly new principle in the bill. It is primarily a rearrangement, a redrafting and a simplification. It seems to me that the most valuable assistance we can get on that phase of it in the banking

That is something that must be done in the House of Commons as a result of budget proposals. This is like consolidating the statutes. If we cannot do the job in committee, all right; but I think we can.
I am one of the members to whom the Minister of Finance referred as not qualified to give expert and understandable study to this bill.
Me, too.

However, the more I heard him explain that, the more disturbed I was about the desirability of the bill going through at this time. He rather suggested that the most valuable contribution to the discussion of this bill must come from lawyers. But lawyers are usually hired to protect the people who are to be taxed; and evidently the minister feels-that having been his profession before he became full-time Minister of Finance-we should be satisfied now if the lawyers who are protecting the big income tax payers approve the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no; I did not say that. Don't make a political speech.
That is the inference which I must draw from what the minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I tried to make the revision of this bill an extremely non-party matter. It is not a question of protecting anybody.
It is definitely a nonparty question as far as I am concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is as far as I am concerned ; and I spent long hours trying to draw up a decent bill.

I am not objecting to that. I am talking about the minister's explanation of the bill. If he had not made that explanation, probably I should not be saying anything at all. I may not be able to appraise the technicalities of the bill, but I am able to appraise fairly quickly what a man says, and to understand what he is talking about.
There is another point. It is said that we could put this bill through the house in a very short time. When the hon. member for Rosedale spoke a minute ago I learned for the first time that we were to begin 5840-311
morning sittings tomorrow. Well, we can put anything through if we have not time to examine it. We could take any number of bills and put them through the house in the same way that you put wheat through a thresher. But that is not the purpose of bringing legislation before the house. You do not bring legislation before the house in order only that it may go through the formal procedure which makes it law. The purpose of bringing a bill before the house is to have it examined here, to satisfy the various interests concerned that it is proper legislation.
I am not so sure that this is the proper time to bring a bill of this kind before us. It cannot, at one and the same time, be an intricate bill and a simple bill. From the minister's explanation it is so intricate that we have not the ability to understand it; and because it is so intricate that we cannot understand it, it is so simple that we should let it go through the house with no examination at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry if I conveyed the impression that it was so intricate we could not understand or appreciate it. I did not intend to suggest that. Anyone who has read the bill will realize that it is a long, technical measure. Actually the bill has been available to every hon. member of the house for almost a year. While it is true that substantial amendments have been made, the broad arrangement and the great majority of the sections are completely unchanged. Anyone who is interested in the bill, whether he is a lawyer or a businessman, a school teacher, or anyone else, has had something like a year to give it detailed and careful study. As I said last year when I introduced the bill. I did so for the purpose of enabling members of parliament and others who were interested to give it study. That is what we have done.
Let me make this second point. I am not attempting to force this or any other bill through the house; but I say we will never get it through the house until we start to consider it. If we embark upon this long discussion at the resolution stage, before having seen the amended version of the bill I introduced a year ago, it seems to me we might as well give up any attempt 'to get one of these revisions or consolidations of the income tax law through the house. That is all I am asking-that I be allowed to introduce this bill. Members of the house can look at it. read it over, study every section, and be prepared to discuss*it either in the banking and commerce committee, if they are members of
Income Tax Act

that committee, or here in committee of the whole. The committee may rest assured that I am not trying to jam this bill through. It is not needed this year, but I believe it is a forward step in improving our legislation. That is all.

In my opinion. Mr. Chairman, this is one measure that should not be forced through the house quickly because time is limited. Apart from the actual tax rates themselves, probably there is nothing which affects the people of Canada more directly than the administration of the Income Tax Act.
The minister indicated that we have had this measure before us for about a year, and implied that we have had ample opportunity to consider it. Later he asserted that, based upon representations made to the government, a great many changes have been made, which of course in effect would nullify his previous assertion that we have had ample opportunity to consider the bill. Moreover, it is one thing to take a bill and study it, and another thing to take a bill when we have an opportunity of asking exactly what certain clauses, phrases and sections mean.
The minister has said that the bill is to go to the banking and commerce committee. I am happy to learn this. If my memory serves me correctly, the minister indicated some months ago, or perhaps it was some weeks ago, that it was not his intention to have this bill referred to a committee of the house. I was disappointed when that announcement was made; therefore I welcome his suggestion that it should go to a committee.
The minister also indicated that it was not desirable to accept representations from organizations and bodies throughout the country which might wish to appear before that committee. That, of course, depends upon the opportunity which those organizations have been given to make their representations; and I understood the minister to say that they have been given ample opportunity to make their submissions.
One thing I think is particularly significant with respect to any income tax law-that is, the actual administration. No doubt the law officers of the crown and other experts will appear before the banking and commerce committee; but will that committee have an opportunity to examine those actually charged with the responsibility of administration? I think a great deal of dissatisfaction has arisen among Canadians during the last number of years because of the indefiniteness of the act, and because of the fact that so many discretions have been exercised under it that actually we have had almost identical cases dealt with 
in different ways in different parts of the country. The minister has said that one purpose of the proposed legislation is to remove many of these discretions. Personally I think it high time this was done, because, as I said a moment ago, we have had a great variety of interpretations and much variation in dealing with almost similar cases in different parts of Canada. In fact it comes to my mind at the moment that in two almost identical cases affecting farmers, one in the Calgary district office and the other in the Edmonton district office, completely opposite interpretations were placed upon the act, and entirely different decisions given.
I appreciate the fact that there may be a great deal of difficulty in drafting an act which would remove all or nearly all those objections, but I do feel that it is desirable to have an act more definite than the legislation under which the people of this country have been labouring for so long. I am more particularly concerned about uniformity of interpretation and application throughout the length and breadth of this country. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, my question is this. Will this committee-of which, incidentally, I am not a member-have an opportunity to call before it those actually engaged in the work of administering the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Unquestionably I would hope that the deputy minister of taxation would be among those who would appear before the committee and explain in detail the administrative sections proposed, as well as the method of administering the act. That is one reason for having the bill considered by the committee on banking and commerce rather than the committee of the whole house.

Perhaps the minister would answer another question along somewhat similar lines. It has to do with calling other interested bodies before the committee to give evidence. The strongest argument in favour of that suggestion is the one advanced by the minister himself as to the desirability of getting the bill through as quickly as possible. He used that argument against calling other bodies before the committee. The minister himself states-and his point has a great deal of merit-that this is the type of bill that the average person has difficulty in understanding or discussing with intelligence. The chief advantage of referring it to the committee on banking and commerce would be to have a full explanation from the experts who will be in charge of administration of the measure. That is important. But the very fact that the members who will constitute the banking and commerce committee are not experts seems

Income Tax Act
to indicate that they should have the benefit of hearing such opposing views as may exist, views in opposition to this, that or the other provision of the bill. If we are to hear from the officials of the department, surely we would wish to hear the views of any who are opposed to the bill. It would not be proper for departmental officials to appear before the committee and say that they believe this is a bad bill.
I know there are some organizations which would wish to have certain provisions modified. And because members of the committee on banking and commerce are to hear the arguments put forward by experts from the department. if the bill is to be considered fairly, we should be allowed to ask other interested organizations throughout the country to appear before the committee and, through their experts, submit their views as to changes or new provisions they might wish to incorporate in the act. This might involve some further time, but the very importance of the bill indicates that we should take the time to hear the evidence of those who may be opposed or who may wish to suggest amendments. I would ask the minister to give us the assurance that that opportunity will be accorded to the committee on banking and commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course that would be a matter for the committee on banking and commerce to consider. The committee will be master of its own procedure.
But a recommendation from the minister would carry weight.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should think it would be impracticable to hear very much evidence at this time. It will be remembered that within the last year many briefs have been filed by a large number of groups. The subject has been well canvassed. If the committee feels that further evidenced should be heard from outside sources, that will be done. But I cannot tell my hon. friend now whether the committee would be prepared to do that, or whether I as a member of the committee- and I do not know whether I am or not; I think I am-would be prepared to make that recommendation. In any event the committee will have to make the decision.
The resolution asks for leave to introduce a bill. All I am asking at this stage is that the committee allow me to present the bill so that they may see what they have to study. I hope that hon. members have already given the bill a great deal of study. Apparently some have not, but I am hoping they will get to work now and study the bill. Then they can decide whether further evidence should be called.

I support the minister and join with him in his appeal that the bill be advanced as quickly as possible. I understand it is complicated, and, if we are to carry our full responsibilities, hon. members should study it from every point of view and secure evidence which may be available.
For years this taxation legislation has been complicated. We have been told that an effort has been made by the officials to simplify it, but I have not yet seen evidence of very much simplification. I believe the bill should be advanced another stage, and that it should be passed. Even if it is not perfect, we can attempt to perfect it in another year. Any change, particularly after the measure has been studied by the officials and by qualified bodies responsible for its administration, will be an improvement over what we now have. Therefore I join with the minister in appealing to the committee of the whole to have the measure advanced so that it may be dealt with and passed at this session. Even though it may not be perfect, we should deal with it.

I support the hon. member for Cumberland in what he has just said. I trust that in the preparation of the bill great care has been taken to prevent any taxpayer from avoiding payment of all the taxes he should pay. The ingenuity of some accountants is amazing. It is extraordinary to find, if one employs the proper accountant, how very well one can get along when, it comes to the payment of income tax. It is nothing short of wonderful how some people can avoid the payment of income tax and still remain within the law. I would mention as an illustration the case of two young men who, we will say, go into the garage business. After they have been in business for a little while they obtain ant exclusive agency for some make of motorcar. They sell a great many cars, with the result that they make a good profit and a good net income. In consequence they have to pay a high tax to the government. That is not quite satisfactory to them, and an expert accountant comes along and says, "You should incorporate, and become a joint stock company." They proceed to form a joint stock company and become incorporated. Then they proceed to sell their exclusive franchise to that joint stock company. In payment they accept a certain number of debentures. When they make their profit the next- year, instead of declaring the net profit they have made they pay off so many of the debentures they hold, with the result that they get out of paying the tax they should pay.
That is only one example. Some of these experts seem to find it easy to get around the law. It is not fair, and it docs not do justice

to the government or to those who are anxious to pay their full amount of taxation. It seems to me it would be of great assistance to us in going over this bill if we could have before us some of those expert accountants who are so ingenious in getting around the law; but I doubt very much whether that would be possible.
I believe we should go ahead with the bill, do the best Ave can with it, and if we find it imperfect, it can be amended in future sessions.

Mr. Chairman, I do not see any objection to supporting the resolution. I think it is most important that such an historic place as the Plains of Abraham and the site of the battle of Ste. Foy be properly preserved. I never go to Quebec City without going out Grande Allee to look over the battleground. It was a remarkable achievement for Wolfe's army to ascend the heights from the St. Lawrence river to the Plains of Abraham during the night and be ready to engage next morning in a conflict which had such momentous results. I think the battlefields commission is doing an excellent job in looking after these sites. It is well laid out; the roads are well taken care of, and every effort is made to beautify the surroundings, which, of course, is what the nation should do.
When the hon. member was speaking to the resolution I asked if any area east of Quebec City was included in the plans, and I understood him to say no. I think the whole of that land where the Montmorency river flows into the St. Lawrence, at which point severe fighting took place between Montcalm and Wolfe and where Wolfe made his first strong attempt to take the city, should be preserved for posterity. I went there, but I do not remember whether the land had been laid out and beautified. Part of the island of Orleans also figured prominently in the fighting, and I should like to know if there is some program for preserving the works established on the island of Orleans, where many of Wolfe's troops were stationed. The same would apply to Point Levis, from where Wolfe made his last ascent up the river. I think it is to the credit of any country that it should preserve and take care of its historic sites, and undoubtedly the Plains of Abraham and the site of the battle of Ste. Foy constitute one of the most historic sites in Canada.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS ADMINISTRATION-PENSIONS FOR WARTIME DISABILITIES

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS ADMINISTRATION-PENSIONS FOR WARTIME DISABILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to voice a grievance and to request redress. The subject of my grievance is certain forgotten victims among Canadian veterans of world wars I and II. As cases in point, I propose to refer to veteran Sholto B. McClellan, No. 77732, now living at 361 Osborne road, North Vancouver, British Columbia, of world war I. and veteran Frank W. Connorton, V52017 (R.C.N.V.R.), now living in Vancouver, British Columbia.
Evidence strongly indicates that each of these veterans is the victim of a serious miscarriage of justice in the matter of pension for wartime disability. My limited experience fills me with anxiety that each of these two men is a representative of a class of victim veterans, the numbers of which are more than disturbing for all Canadians. May I give some particulars about McClellan? In a letter dated May 31, 1948, he writes as follows:
What we are complaining about is that our records have been mishandled, or, in real truth, falsified, to make it look as if we were not entitled to pensions.
My evidence clearly shorvs that the charges are true.
Concerning McClellan. Walter H. Kirehner, secretary of the Canadian combat veterans' association, in a letter dated April 5, 1948, had this to say:
What has taken place in respect to the McClellan ease (since the commissioners under P.C. 4980 made their findings) is what will
Veterans A flairs

take place within the claims of all those I represent-as their legal adviser-until such time as the actual, recorded evidence given before the inquiry by my witnesses receives scrutiny by a properly-qualified judicial body familiar with the implications of the military pensions legislation statutes of Canada.
And again I quote from the same document:
My witnesses were those I produced to back up the charges of definite infringements of the military pension statutes or what is termed "maladministration" illustrated in bureaucratic violation of the statutes, by the use of improper or false reports read into the records-and the rights of ex-service men and women and their dependents so outlawed.
McClellan contends that he was given only a 50 per cent pension for a 100 per cent multiple war disability condition. He says that, as a disability pensioner, he took up fruit ranching and invested $5,000 in a ranch under the soldier settlement board, and was evicted from the ranch on account of temporary arrears during the depression period, when such arrears could have been waived under the provisions of the Soldier 'Settlement Act owing to McClellan's disabilities. Subsequently he sought damages in the exchequer court for wrongful eviction and recovery of his $5,000 equity, but without result.
Again, at seventy-two years of age-and it must be remembered that we are speaking of a man who went and risked his life for Canada in world war I-in order to keep a roof over his head and that of his wife, he is forced to wash dishes in an hotel. He received an injury to his leg while working, but the workmen's compensation board of British Columbia refuse to honour the claim as they state that, while the injury prevents McClellan from carrying on his employment, the injury would be only a superficial one to a young or middle-aged man: but the arthritic condition and allied disabilities arising from war service, coupled with McClellan's age, make the outcome of this injury a responsibility of the Canadian pension commission.
This helps us to see how some of these splendid men are getting what is popularly called "the run-around".
Again, unless McClellan is given his proper pension assessment of 100 per cent instead of the present 50 per cent, he will be compelled to sell the equity they have in their home and endeavour to make both ends meet by living on the proceeds, because he is definitely out of the labour market, as his private physician's report makes clear.
May I turn now from the McClellan case and consider briefly matters pertaining to Frank W. Connorton, who is just a boy. This man enlisted on January 5, 1943. He was well, strong, sound in body and mind and full of

hope for a future of abundant living. He was discharged on March 18, 1946, as medically unfit, broken in mind and body, with no hope for a future of any kind or degree of abundant living. After months of striving for justice, he became the subject of a Canadian pension ruling signed at Ottawa, May 10, 1947. In this ruling appear the following words:
The commission rules:
"Prespomlylolisthesis-pre-enlistment	condition, aggravated three-fifths during service in Canada. Effective June 1, 1946, as the aggravation did not arise out of nor was it directly connected with military service."
After months more of struggle, he was again the victim, receiving in a letter dated January 29, 1948, the following message:
I have to inform you that the reports of the examination recently held on you show that your pensionable disability from prespondylolisthesis is 18 per cent in extent.
That letter, dated January 29, 1948, is signed by W. E. Dexter, secretary of the Canadian pension commission.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that this young man receives no more than $20 a month, if I interpret it aright, to recompense him for practically total wreckage in war service to Canada. How did it come about that such a gruesome state of affairs developed in Canada as is illustrated in the case of this young man?
Reviewing Connorton's case, I find myself impelled to ask the minister to find the answer for me to four main pertinent questions. First, did this man's condition partly result from an appendix operation in June, 1943? In this operation, I might say, the man was given a local anaesthetic through a needle thrust into the spine. But the man administering the anaesthetic was apparently practising on Connorton; he had to make eight attempts before he was able to get the needle into the right place in the spine, the whole process being accompanied by excruciating pain and what later developed to be permanent injury to the young man.
The second question: Did his tragic final condition partly result from his effort to do work for which surgical bungling had unfitted him?
Third: Did his condition result in any considerable measure from a spinal fusion operation on November 15, 1945, apparently unsuccessful, and subsequent mismanagement on the part of government officials in the army?
Fourth:	Was his misfortune partly the
result of a second unsuccessful spinal fusion operation on or about September 18, 1946?
I become more suspicious and inquisitive in regard to this case when I review again Frank W. Connorton's history of hospitalization. As given to me it is as follows:

Veterans Affairs
1.	Local spinal anaesthetic given the latter part of June, 1943, when the needle was driven eight times into the spine by a Doctor Palmer, followed by an appendix operation.
2.	Hospitalized for gland trouble in the spring of 1944.
3.	Given a one-man medical board by Doctor Whitelaw, July, 1944. X-rays taken of his back; then the report coming back- and I draw the attention of hon. members of the committee particularly to this finding, which has an important bearing on the finding of the commission on May 10, 1947- "Nothing wrong with the spine". Then he was classified by this board as A-l.
4.	He was examined by Doctor Mackenzie at the Givenchy barracks, August, 1944, who reported also, "Nothing wrong with the spine".
5.	He was admitted to Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver, B.C., August, 1944, with a condition diagnosed as bronchitis and laryngitis. This condition diagnosed by Doctor Harold and an operation for tonsilitis performed by Doctor Jackson.
6.	Examined by Doctor Ross Robertson, neurosurgeon, on complaints of Connorton regarding the condition of his spine. This physician told the man he had an unmatured spine. He was given a first spinal fusion on November 15, 1945, by this surgeon.
7.	On April 2, 1946. he was boarded by the neurosurgeons Boucher, Naden, Starr, Thompson and Black, on complaints of the man that he was still suffering from pain in his back.
8.	He was turned over by the neurosurgeons to the departmental psychiatrist, Doctor Stanley, who stated in his board: "Nothing wrong with the man except in his imagination".
9.	X-rays taken of the man's spine at the Nanaimo hospital about the middle of September, 1946, on complaints of the man that his back was bothering him.
10.	He was examined by Doctor Frank Lehman, neurosurgeon, Shaughnessy hospital, about the middle of September, 1946.
11.	He was boarded by the neurosurgeons Boucher, Naden, Starr, Thompson and Chip-suik. Exploratory operation of opening up the spine followed and discovered bone-graft fusion did not take. The second spinal fusion operation followed.
I think almost every member of the committee must be astonished by the history of this man's hospitalization. Note particularly that on July 4 Doctor Whitelaw declared there was nothing wrong with the spine, and that in August. 1944, Doctor Mackenzie also declared there was nothing wrong with the
spine. Let us bear in mind that the commission found that the man suffered from pre-enlistment disability; yet these two doctors declared there was nothing wrong with the spine in 1944! This ought to be enough to show that there should be some effort at consistency among those employed by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Then Doctor Ross Robertson found an unmatured spine, right after these other two doctors had declared there was nothing wrong with the spine! Then a spinal fusion operation took place, a major operation which, I understand, is most painful and most dangerous. Then Doctor Stanley, psychiatrist, declared there was nothing wrong with the man except in his imagination.
I wonder how many of these pestilential psychiatrists we have in the employ of the Department of Veterans Affairs. In a general, sweeping way I would stop here to advise the veterans affairs department to clear out these people as one would clear vermin out of a house. I do not think we have any use for psychiatrists to deal with our soldiers in this dominion; and I do not care who the psychiatrists are. If what they do is indicated lay what was done in this case I believe everyone will agree that I have not spoken immoderately. Here is a man who, in the face of a spinal fusion operation, declares that the soldier has nothing wrong with his back except in his imagination! Hon. members will recall that there was an exploratory operation opening the spine, which disclosed that the bone-graft fusion had not taken; and this immediately followed the declaration of our psychiatrist that the only thing wrong with the man's spine was in his mind! If we should have another war, and if any of us should have a boy going to that war, I think we should offer a silent prayer that he will never fall into the hands of a psychiatrist.
Then, on May 10, 1947, after all this, the pension commission found there was nothing to indicate that his condition was caused by military service! Probably there was a play on "military service" as a pair of weasel words, so that what the commission said was technically accurate but in spirit monstrously wrong. If this man's ills did not result from service in His Majesty's forces, I do not know how in the world one would proceed to prove that fact. While all this is going on, the boy called Connorton, who might be your boy or mine, Mr. Speaker, a lad in whom our whole faith and hope are reposed, is wrecked. One of God's noble youth in Canada is destroyed.
*1906
Veterans Affairs

The question we ask-and I speak for all members of the house-is this: What is to be done about this boy? This house, with one voice, asks the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) to tell us what is to be done about this boy? He was taken away from home-healthy, gloriously strong, able to do heavy work. I have evidence in abundance to prove that. He was taken into the army, and was turned out of it a wreck. And it was at that time it was declared that his disability was the result of pre-enlistment deficiency. He was turned out, thrown on the scrap heap, with a miserable $20 a month-not enough to provide him with a room.
What is to be done with the others in his class? This boy is not the only one. Where one has suffered, there are plenty of others. Who is going out to find them in all their various theatres of suffering? Who is going to do something to see that their injustices are remedied?
The suffering of each of these two boys, these two servicemen Connorton and McClellan, is extreme now. The veteran Con-noiton, for example, has a disablement from spinal fusion, an exceedingly serious and painful malady.
I received today this letter dated June 8, 1948, which deals with spinal fusion cases:
John Blaekmore, Esq., H P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa
Dear Mr. Blaekmore:
re Spinal Elision cases
In my conversation during the 1947 parliamentary session with Brig. Gen. W. P. Warner, M.D., director general of the treatment services of the D.V.A., in discussing the plight of the spinal-fusion cases, he admitted that "once a man received a spinal fusion," as he expressed himself, "God Almighty could not cure him"; or, in other words, restore the man to a physical condition where he could again render ablebodied service in industry or the professions, such as civil engineering, where men are subject to physical strains.
General Warner further stated that while he considered the treatment services of the department "the finest in the dominion" yet, as he expressed himself, "the spinalfusion cases were the great nightmare of the treatment services."
If you will refer to General Warner's report, incorporated in the findings of the public inquiry, held under P.C. 4986, and embodied in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the select committee on veterans affairs, April 15, 1948, it will be observed he is quite frank in acknowledging the gravity of the situation confronting men who have received one, two or more spinal fusions with resultant near-total disability.
Yours sincerely,
Walter H. Kirchner, Secretary,
Canadian Combat Veterans' Assn.

Here is this boy expected to make his own living, turned out roughly and provided with $20 a month, which is not enough to supply him with his medical needs. What is to be done about him? Is there any ear in the Dominion of Canada; are there any ears in the House of Commons, which will attune themselves to his pleading voice, and resolve that something shall be done to make right this monstrous wrong?
I would ask the minister to prepare at an early day detailed answers to the questions I have asked, and to give them to the house either before or when his estimates come up for discussion. I would ask the minister to have the most exacting investigation made of the various decisions which have been made, bearing upon each of these twro cases, and to explain to the house fully at an early day the justification for the decisions of May 10, 1947, and January 29, 1948, in respect of the Connorton case and the corresponding decisions in the McClellan case.
I would ask the minister, further, to tell the house at an early day what he proposes to do (1) to remedy the injustices in each of these two cases; (2) to seek out and remedy the injustices in each of the cases in that class of injustices of which Connorton and McClellan are examples and (3) to safeguard other cases throughout this land against similar injustices.
May I assure the minister I intend to follow these cases through, in the hope of my being of some assistance to the minister in his efforts to detect and to remedy certain abuses in the administration of veterans affairs which have left many results deeply regrettable to all Canadians.

speechtext:
I should like to know the number of applications that have been made for citizenship certificates by native-born Canadians since the new act came into effect. When the act was first established there were, in different parts of the country, ceremonies which had a profound effect upon the attitude of our citizens who had come from other lands. There were public functions, and an endeavour was made to educate our people in the meaning of citizenship, not only from the point of view of its benefits and rights but also as to its responsibilities. Much was made of the fact that many Canadians would desire to have certificates in order to show that they were in fact citizens of this country, without regard to hyphenate considerations. That was most commendable. I think the citizenship act has had a most salutary effect upon our people as a whole.
However, I feel that the department, since the act came into effect, has not been as enthusiastic about it as it was at the time it originally became law. I should like to have from the minister the number of native-born Canadians who have applied for citizenship certificates in the years 1947 and 1948 to date. Second, I should like to know the number of those who were naturalized as Canadian citizens prior to the act coming into effect, who have since asked for and secured citizenship certificates.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

I have
the figures for the previous year, but for the year 1947-48 natural-born Canadians who were entitled to certificates in proof of citizenship applied to a total number of 11,972. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Is the minister
satisfied with the degree to which applications have been made, particularly by naturalized citizens? What has been done to encourage applications for these certificates?
Supply-Secretary of State

Could the minister advise the committee as to the extent to which the enthusiasm that existed in January, 1947, in his department, has waned in the intervening months?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I would not say that it has waned in the slightest degree. A person who has a naturalization certificate has no need of a certificate in proof of citizenship. If he turns in his naturalization certificate, wTe issue the other certificate if he wishes it, but his naturalization certificate is of equal value. Some people may ask, what is the value of having a certificate in proof of citizenship? If you . are travelling abroad it is of value as proof of citizenship, and it can be of use when returning to this country.
There has been a great increase in the number applying for citizenship in this country. During the last year we issued 25,691 certificates. This is about ninety certificates for each working day, which is quite a creditable performance considering the investigation that is required. These certificates are not sold like postage stamps, because the application must be carefully examined. I feel that the citizenship registration office is doing a good' work and has been most efficient during the past year.
