speechtext:
I do not want to delay the passage of the minister's estimates, but last year I happened to be absent temporarily from the house when they were up and when I wanted1 to ask a couple of questions. One has to do with the patent office and the other with regard to the citizenship registration branch. Many young people find it quite difficult, under the Patent Act as amended, to secure a patent for their useful invention, owing to the cost of the patent and their not having cash to pay for it. A great many young people have to go to the United States for those very good reasons because they find it less, difficult to secure a patent and sell their patent there, and Canada thus loses their talent.
Second, how is the citizenship registration plan working out? A great many people have the idea, and it is generally understood in the old country, that we are no longer British subjects but Canadian citizens only. I remember when the Athenia was sunk in the early days of the last war. There were 130 Canadians on board, and someone suggested that they were British subjects, which meant a lot on the seas. I think the minister should state that Canadian citizens are still British subjects. Remember civis romanus sum and
[Jlr. Diefenbaker.]
what it meant, as being a British subject did on the seven seas.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The act still provides that a Canadian citizen is a British subject. It is true that an act has been introduced at Westminster, framed somewhat along the lines of our own citizenship act, which provides that residents of the United Kingdom and the colonies will be known as citizens of the United Kingdom and colonies. The fact remains that in Canada we are not only Canadian citizens but also British subjects.
The hon. member asked how the citizenship program is working out. We have had the greatest co-operation from judges across the country. There was a time when applicants for naturalization were called before a court, answered a few perfunctory questions, the application was approved, and the certificate issued. There was little formality about the proceedings. Now throughout the country we have formalities which are designed to impress the new Canadians when they receive their citizenship certificates. The judges have taken great interest in this work, and have received the co-operation of service clubs and particularly from the Daughters of the Empire, who come to these ceremonies and assist in making the new Canadians feel they are welcome in this country. I have attended a large number of these ceremonies, and consider that they help to give the new Canadian a realization of the importance of the step he is taking and make him realize that he is assuming obligations as well as the privileges of citizenship.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I was bom in Canada, as were my parents, and I have not taken out any citizenship papers for the reason that I could not see why I, born a Canadian, needed to take out citizenship papers. But if I wanted to go to England and then to the continent of Europe, after I obtain my passport as a Canadian born in this country, do I have to take out any more papers than I did before?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No; the passport is sufficient.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I want to clear up a misunderstanding created as a result of a question regarding citizenship that I asked in this house on May 19. I asked a question as to one Dimitri Dontzow, now a resident of Montreal. My question was to the effect, where was he during the first world war; was he now engaged in work for the government, and had he taken any steps toward

Criminal Code
securing Canadian citizenship? The answer given was that he entered Canada on January 7. 1948, and was granted non-immigrant status. The manner in which my question was drafted was designed to prevent any harm or hurt from being done to that man. I was totally unaware of the fact that a controversy was going on among some groups as to whether he should be entitled to remain in Canada and become a citizen. I have always followed the course of not doing anything to injure any person through the protection granted to me by my parliamentary privilege, and I feel that, in asking that question. I have done some harm to that man. While I have not undertaken to say this, I want to say that, so far as I am concerned, this man would make a good Canadian citizen, that he was and has been a consistent enemy of communism in the Ukraine, where he operated since the war, and that those who today in this country are endeavouring to secure his deportation are doing so because they resent the work he did on behalf of democracy during the war and following. I think it is only fair, sir, to mention that, because a lot has been said on this question, indicating, as it might, that I was endeavouring to do harm to a man who, according to information I have gained, not only from members of his organization but from independent Canadians of undoubtedly first-rate reputation, would in my opinion make a good prospective citizen and is a man who ought to be given honourable sanctuary in Canada.
May I ask the minister whether the British government has communicated with him as Secretary of State with a view to ascertaining whether or not a new form of citizenship should be established to be known as commonwealth citizenship rather than as British or empire citizenship?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The British government does not communicate with my department; it communicates through the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I believe there have been some communications discussing the form of title that should be applied to a subject of the British commonwealth, but I do not know what reply, if any, the Department of External Affairs might have sent.

speechtext: Would the minister obtain that information?

Yes, I shall be glad to do so.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of Bill No. 207, to amend the criminal code (pistols, motor vehicles, level crossings and the payment of fines).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to detain the house for more than a few minutes in discussing this bill. I would point out, however, that this is the 101st day of the session, and I think we should have devoted an hour to the discussion of the questions involved in the bill. The loss of life in Canada is simply appalling. We find that in one instance eighteen persons are killed in the space of a week end, and in every newspaper that one picks up its pages are figuratively coloured red with the blood of men, women and children who have been ruthlessly slaughtered by motor vehicles.
This bill does not conflict with the bill which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) introduced on Monday, since it deals with different subject matters in every section. The bill now before the house is No. 207, copies of which are on the table.
I shall not speak for more than twelve minutes, and in that time I wish to refer to three or four important principles that are involved in the bill. In 1935 there was a learned discussion in this house, lasting the whole of one day and the day following, and I might say that a committee consisting of both houses of parliament was appointed in England to investigate this entire subject.
Coming to this particular bill, I think the object at which it aims is quite clear. On almost every highway in Canada there has been slaughter of innocent people, men, women and children, and that is true right across the country; yet little or nothing is done about it.
Speaking in this house on March 9, 1937, I stated that if any devastating disease were to take the toll the motorcar is taking by night and by day, science and medicine would know no rest until they had found a cure. The death toll by the motorcar constitutes Canada's greatest scandal. The slaughter goes on all over the country, and the economic losses are appalling. The worst thing about it is, I think, the indifference of the public.
In that discussion a great many other matters were referred to. On that occasion I
Criminal Code

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
quoted the observations of Chief Justice Rose at the winter assizes in 1937. in his address to the grand jury. Chief Justice Rose is reported as follows:
"The toll of life by motors is appalling and the number of people injured is infinitely greater," declared Chief Justice Rose in his address to the grand jury this afternoon.
"Careless driving will stop just as soon as the people of Ontario make up their minds that it is to stop," he continued.
It is the part of juries to see that there are convictions. If lawbreakers get the idea there will not be convictions they will continue.
His lordship said there appeared to be something illogical in the fact that a motorist who kills gets a term in prison, while another who is merely fortunate enough to injure his victim gets off easily.
As I have said, five years before that time, in the old country, a committee of both houses of parliament was set up to go into this question and it got something done. On February 13, 1935, there was a non-political debate on the subject in the Canadian house on a resolution of mine in which some twenty-seven members took part. In that debate I emphasized the fact that one of the commandments is, "Thou shalt not kill", but many men of real worth have violated the laws not only of God but of man.
No invention has contributed more to the education, pleasure and enjoyment of the people than the motorcar; but its use is one thing, its abuse another. As with every great invention, use and abuse are two distinct things. During the past century scientific discoveries in medicine, chemistry and physics have resulted in untold good to humanity, but the abuse of some of these discoveries in chemistry, biochemistry and physics has in war proved a curse to mankind. In Jike manner today the abuse of the motorcar is a curse to humanity.
On looking into this question, one finds involved in it tremendous annual losses in deaths, accidents, injuries and money. Untold sorrow and suffering are caused, intense pain and grief exceeding anything that the human imagination can conceive. The only evils which have equalled it are plague, pestilence and famine, battle, murder and sudden death. It would be misleading and mischievous to attribute all the blame for these ghastly horrors on our highways to all who drive and use motorcars. Ninety-five per cent of the drivers want to obey the law; it is the five percent about whom I am complaining.
One has to study the records to know the facts, and as I study the records of thousands of cases I am driven to the conclusion that, beyond dispute, this small minority must take

the major part of the blame. They appear to have exploited for their own pleasure or profit the generous tolerance of others by using their cars in an irresponsible, careless, cruel and un-Christian way. The fault is grievous, and they can have no ground for complaint if they are put under restraint as far as the criminal code is concerned. Ignorance and thoughtlessness are no palliatives. Obedience is the only reparation they can make and it is long overdue.
I should like to quote something that was said by the late Chief Justice Meredith, who so ably presided on circuit for nearly forty-six years. At the last assizes over which he presided in Toronto he addressed the grand jury on the amendments that were made in 1930. He said:
And as now nearly everyone is a car owner and car driver, young and old, of all sorts and conditions, it is difficult to get justice in even a civil action.
Car-driver-jurors have nearly all the speed fever; and self-preservation instincts are so strong that they will not be persuaded to decide against drivers who have been no more unlawful than they themselves often, if not commonly, are.
What then is the remedy? I think it should be:	Make the laws plain and reasonably
severe and enforce them; and cancel licences freely.
And at the other end of the matter: Give no licence to anyone who is not proved to be mentally and physically, and from experience and a knowledge of the highway laws, thoroughly capable.
A situation such as this calls for a united effort from the church, the press, parliament, the legislatures, boards of trade, chambers of commerce and all other public bodies. The privation and sorrow, the broken lives and shattered homes, resulting from such a holocaust are just as real as at the time of the nation's supreme trial in the war. It is hidden, and it is suffered in silence; but how long will that continue to be?
Three features dominate the conduct of motor traffic: a domineering indifference to the convenience of others, excessive speed, and congestion. Ever since man learned to direct a machine more powerful than himself, he has asserted his superiority of force over his neighbours. "Make way or take the consequences" has been his cry. Yet this indifference to others is limited to a small number of motor drivers. The motor leagues of the provinces make the same complaint. It is a small number out of the large body of drivers who transgress; ninety-nine per cent of them respect and obey the law. The majority of motorcar drivers have only a hazy knowledge of the mechanism of their machine, and for absolute control the only condition in which a car is fit to be driven at thirty miles an hour

Criminal Code
is perfect adjustment. Even so, the machine is potentially as dangerous as a loaded gun and must be handled with equal care and vigilance. A moment's inattention may be fraught with dire results. Every motor vehicle is a dangerous implement, even when controlled by the most expert, and requires incessant vigilance in all circumstances, especially at speeds above thirty miles an hour.
Transportation should be a means to an end, not an end in itself. I could go on further, but I will not do so.
I come now to the bill itself. The first section deals with the use of pistols or air-guns, loaded or unloaded. Pistols can be purchased at many places. I know of an industry on Spadina avenue that sends out pictures and pamphlets describing its manufacture. They come over the border from Connecticut, in the United States, and it is easy to buy one.
Another section provides that "pistol" shall include anything of the shape or form or size of a pistol. Many of these fatal accidents have been caused as a result of the ease with which a pistol may be secured, especially by some of the younger people. The pistol, added to the abuse of the motorcar, is a menace to the people of this country.
My time is about up, but I may say that another section deals with those who drive motorcars under the influence of alcohol. That is a practice which has been condemned at many sittings of the courts by the Ontario government's expert, Doctor Rogers. He says that liquor is killing five people and injuring eighty-four every week on the highways of Ontario alone. I think the opposition members should look into this matter. This is referred to in Hansard of April 22, 1947. I propose an amendment under one section of this bill.
Every section deals with a different principle. Subsection 4 of section 55 of the criminal code as enacted uses the word "narcotic". I propose to substitute "under the influence of alcohol", so that the section will then read:
Everyone who, while under the influence of alcohol or any narcotic, drives any motor vehicle or automobile is guilty of an offence and liable to . . .
And the punishment is set out.
The next matter dealt with is the hit-and-run drivers, the most cowardly type of all. I have seen instances on the main streets of our city where a hit-and-run driver comes along and injures someone. I was on Danforth avenue yesterday and I saw a small child on the road. Several cars passed her, and the last one came along at an outrageous rate of speed and knocked her down. Nobody could stop him. In fact a special policeman would be
necessary for each car for that purpose. But these hit-and-run drivers get away with it. No one got that man's number. Yet the child was injured. Many children have been killed and injured in this way. In our city, in the riding which I represent, and it is an industrial riding at the south end, there are some poor people whose children have been knocked down and killed by hit-and-run drivers, and no penalty is meted out. It is a form of murder and there should be further legislation dealing with it.
Another matter dealt with in the bill is the failure to stop at level crossings. Several people were killed on Monday at one of these. I should like to have put in the code a section which would read:
The operator of a motor vehicle on street, road, highway or other public place who neglects to come to a full stop before reaching a level crossing where a railway crosses such street, road, highway or other public place, and who does not look and listen for an approaching train before passing a level crossing, shall be guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $50.
The loss of life at level crossings is appalling, and some remedy should be found.
Another section provides that those who cause death are not to drive for two years. It deals with culpable negligence. Under the law of New York state it is for the jury to say. It takes two people to make any accident that I know of on the highway. You cannot have any accident unless two people are involved, one going one way and one another. The cause of death is for the junto say. In some cases they assess the negligence at 20 per cent or 25 per cent on one side and 75 or SO per cent on the other. If the jury brings in a verdict like that, the accused person is not to drive for a period of two years.
Another matter dealt with in the bill is the trial of a young person. The other day in county court in the county of Peel, we had an instance of the trial of a young offender. I believe the parents should be notified in these cases. I do not see why, when one is in Montreal or in another place, the parents should not be notified of their being held in custody for some offence.
The late Chief Justice Rose referred to the present law at the assizes in Toronto; I quoted him a moment ago. He said that the jury was to blame in some cases for not having the courage to enforce the law. The function of a judge is to explain the law to the jury, and the jury is bound to take what the judge says is the law. But in a charge to a jury I believe that, in these cases of manslaughter arising out of the operation of motor vehicles,
Criminal Code

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
the question of fact whether the accused is guilty or not guilty should be left to the jury. On the trial with a jury of persons who cause death or serious injury, it is desirable that the functions of the jury should not be curtailed or abolished. There has been much criticism of many cases of gross, negligence having been taken from the jury. The jury is required to take the law to be what the judge says it is. In many cases trial by junis almost negatived; there are so many loopholes, and many persons guilty of gross negligence get off. I contend that the law should be brought up to date to meet changed conditions. The remainder of this particular Bill No. 207, and some of the members have not read it or seen it, probably, refers to the summary convictions act in England, whereby time is given to pay the fine. This is the 101st day of the session and this is the first opportunity we have had of bringing the bill up for second reading. We are almost back in the days of "Little Dorritt" in Dickens, having regard to the number of people who have been sent to jail under the present system for not paying their fines. Many of them are minor offenders who have never been in jail before in their lives or appeared in court. I believe this is a good provision. The bill provides for time to pay, as is the case under the law of England, where half the prisons have been closed by this wise method of law reform there.
That is all I have to say about the bill. I believe the house should have given more attention to this bill in the early days of the session. There is no reason why we should not have more time to discuss these important matters of life and death to our citizens. It is only necessary to read the newspapers to learn daily about all these deaths which have taken place, not only from level crossing accidents but from motorcar accidents, drown-ings, fires in homes, children left alone and many other causes, floods and fires. This is one of the matters that should be looked into by parliament.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PISTOLS, MOTOR CARS, LEVEL CROSSINGS AND PAYMENT OP FINES
speechtext:
I have not much to say on this bill, Mr. Speaker, except to comment on one or two things the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) had to say as he went along. The bill is a lengthy one, and one would almost need to be a lawyer to follow through all its ramifications and understand it. Some of the penalties proposed in the bill are somewhat drastic.
When the hon. member was commenting on the bill. I was interested in the observations he had to make with regard to accidents at

level crossings. His argument was that certain penalties should be applied where a driver fails to stop, look and listen at a level crossing. I do not think an amendment to the criminal code is the solution of that particular problem. I think level crossings should first be eliminated as far as possible. That is the responsibility of both federal and provincial governments, in the protection of the public. However, until such time as we can get around to the elimination of level crossings, I think the railroads, both short and main lines, should be compelled to place signals at level crossings. In driving through this country, I see hundreds of these level crossings which you come upon suddenly; you do not know a crossing is there until you are on top of it.
I remember being in New Brunswick a year ago, driving along behind a small car. An electric train came out of the woods suddenly and smashed the little car ahead of us, killing an old man who had been riding in it and badly injuring the driver. I was sufficiently intex-ested to go back to that little town that night and listen to the inquest, for I was reasonably sure that if the little car had not been ahead of us we would have been on the crossing and would have been struck by the train coming out of the woods, since there was no warning and no signal. It is the responsibility of the railroads to erect signals of some kind at crossings like that. I heard the jury bring in a verdict in that case, and in their verdict no blame was attached to the railroad, despite the fact that there was no signal and no warning of any kind.
I wanted to make just this comment because of the argument by the sponsor of this bill that the criminal code should be amended to make it an offence, carrying pretty heavy penalties, for anyone on the highway failing to stop, look and listen at a level crossing. In some of the provinces of Canada you may cross the main line of the railway a dozen times in a hundred miles, where you criss-cross back and forth. All these crossings are bad and dangerous; but that is not a condition which can be remedied by legislation. In my opinion it is the responsibility of federal and provincial governments to eliminate such crossings where possible, and to compel the operators of short lines, particularly, to erect warning signals where they cross heavily travelled main highways.
Mr. JOHN R. MacNICOL (Davenport): In the first place, Mr. Speaker. I think the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) deserves credit for his indefatigable energy in endeavouring to protect the public in one way and another, and I for one congratulate him.

Criminal Code
I want to add a word or two to what has been said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), with much of which I agree. The problem is to have someone eliminate level crossings. The responsibility is that of the railways and the provinces and, I presume, also the federal authorities. We have an act on our books, and we vote a good deal of money for the elimination of level crossings; but, even so,
I do not think any of us will live long enough to see all level crossings eliminated.
There are some very bad crossings of this kind. I have in mind one between Brampton and Georgetown, on No. 7 highway, where many cars pass daily. I was almost run into by a train there, because you do not see the train coming from the left, and you are on the track almost before you know it. So anything this house, the legislatures and the railways can do to eliminate level crossings should be done.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PISTOLS, MOTOR CARS, LEVEL CROSSINGS AND PAYMENT OP FINES
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this bill, Mr. Speaker, which is very much like the bill introduced with the same subject matter last year by the hon. member. At that time I had not introduced the annual amendments to the criminal code, and I intimated that some of the ideas contained in the bill would be incorporated in those amendments. Apart from one of those ideas, however, I do not think there was any such incorporation in the amendments to the criminal code last year. That one related to the first two sections of the bill, having reference to the use of firearms and imitation firearms. In the criminal code amendments of last year, which are found in chapter 55 of the statutes of 1947, section 15 provides:
Paragraph (e) of section four hundred and forty-six of the said act is repealed and the following substitued therefor:-
"(c) being armed with an offensive weapon or instrument or imitation thereof robs, or assaults with intent to rob, any person."
I suspect that my hon. friend's objective was to prevent robbery brought about by the use either of a weapon or an imitation weapon, though the amendments proposed in the bill which he introduced last year, and which he has reintroduced this year, do not attain that objective. As far as it is possible to do anything effectively by legislation, I think it was done by the amendment to the criminal code introduced in 1947, which I have cited.
The matter of the use of imitation weapons is only one of a large number of unrelated provisions contained in the bill before the house. It is not possible to discuss the principle of the bill without discussing some of
these unrelated subjects dealt with in the bill. Part of the bill is devoted to a stiffening of the penalties and a change in the law with respect to the driving of motor vehicles by intoxicated persons. Undoubtedly there is a large loss of life on account of the driving of automobiles by persons who are intoxicated. Last year, when the amendments to the criminal code were being considered, the government gave some thought and spent some time in trying to decide whether it would be possible to make the law more effective in that regard. The conclusions we came to were that it would hardly be defensible to adopt the principle my hon. friend has argued for tonight; that is, that it should be an offence to drive an automobile while under the influence of alcohol only.
The reasons for that were stated in some remarks I made on criminal code amendments on July 3, 1947, which are to be found in Hansard of that date at page 5034. The passage is not very long, and I am going to ask the house to be indulgent enough to let me read it, because this is an important subject, and upon reading over these remarks, as I have recently, I find that they represent my views today:
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) referred to an important subject, namely the question of driving motor ears by persons who are intoxicated. This is a matter of increasing importance. With the increasing amount of liquor being consumed in Canada, the increasing drink bill of the Canadian people, the increasing numbers of motorcars on the highways and the increasing number of accidents, parliament should take any steps it can which would be effective to prevent the causing of accidents or deaths on the highways.
Much thought has been given to the matter without. I must admit, very great results in the bill. The penalties for hit-and-run drivers have been increased.
And, may I interject, those penalties were increased by our criminal code amendments last year. They are not as severe as those proposed by the hon. member in his bill tonight; but, as I have had occasion to point out to the house before, penalties may be so severe that convictions cannot be obtained. That is a consideration which I would call to the hon. member's attention. Then, on that occasion I continued:
That is a peculiarly unpleasant sort of offence. We thought we would be justified in recommending an increase in the penalty. On the other hand, we did not think we would accomplish anything by increasing penalties for drunken driving. At the present time th.=- penalties for drunken driving are seven days or thirty days, as the case may be. I. personally, do not think that raising it to fourteen days or sixty days would act as a deterrent.
Criminal Code

There again, I believe Chat many of those persons convicted of drunken driving dread the seven days or the thirty days in jail just as much as they would the -longer periods. If we make the detention longer magistrates and courts become increasingly reluctant to make convictions. In some cases they are reluctant no\c to convict. So we turned our attention from penalties to definitions, and considered how best we could define intoxication. The present definitions could possibly be made more satisfactory. The ordinary definition of intoxication in relation to drivers is that degree of intoxication or of being under the influence of liquor which renders the driving of a car dangerous to the public. This means that if the person were permitted to drive the ear it would be a danger to the public.
That is accepted by most of the eourts. Therefore there did not seem to be much to be gained by trying to extend that definition. It is almost impossible to say that a man is intoxicated if he has had a drink we will say, within one hour, two hours, three hours or four hours, because the variation is so great. It would be extremely severe to make it an offence to drive am automobile while under the influent'- of liquor. Tile courts have ruled that a person is under the influence of liquor -after he has had a drink. The influence may be quite slight, and it hardly seems sufficient to make a criminal out of a man who has had a drink.
I think I should have said that it hardly seems appropriate to make a criminal out of a man who has a drink. Then I continued:
So we abandoned that.
We gave consideration to the reversal of the onus in some cases. The best section that I could evolve, and which I want to put on record for the consideration of members, is this:
"Provided that whenever a motor vehicle is involved in an accident, evidence that the person driving the said motor vehicle acted at or about the time of the accident in a manner indicating that he was under the influence of intoxicating liquor, shall be prima facie evidence that -the said person was intoxicated."
I am not recommending it at this session, but if in the course of time it is found that we have to do something, from what consideration I have been able to give the matter, this is the most practical amendment I ea-n suggest if an amendment is to be made to stiffen the section. The proposed amendment has much to commend itself, but it also has much against it. I should like those who are interested in the subject to give it some consideration between this and the next session. I may say that we have bail strong representations to the effect that we ought to go quite far in amending the section. I have not gone very far. as will be seen when the section is reached; what I have done is to try to offset the decision of the courts with regard to one particular phase of the matter which will be explained when the section is reached.
May I say that the proviso, which was so carefully drafted and upon which I invited comment, elicited no comment whatever either in the house or out of it. Therefore I am unable to suggest any better improvement of the section in question. I really am of the
rilr. Ilsley.]
opinion that to go as far as my hon. friend seeks to go in his bill would be going too far, and would move the criminal law of the country out beyond the proper realm of criminal law; and perhaps would do more harm than good.
As I said, in the bill there are a number of other sections dealing with a variety of subjects. I could take them up one at a time, but I doubt whether my hon. friend expects the house to pass the bill tonight. The discussion has served some useful purpose. He has brought these important matters before the house and the public, and has given hon. members an opportunity to express themselves with respect to them. I cannot accept the bill. At the same time, perhaps when the criminal code amendments come up, and a general discussion of the sections takes place, it may be that something can be done by returning to this bill at that time.
Therefore I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks concerning the matter which is now up for discussion, namely the abolition of appeals to the privy council. It may be that I shall repeat, under some form or other,

Supreme Court Act
certain arguments which have already been submitted during the debate, but there is no harm in that. Some truths are like nails: one must hammer at them repeatedly in order to drive them in well.

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Today the great majority of Canadians are in favour of abolishing appeals to the privy council. In fact, since the Statute of Westminster, it is admitted that the dominions are independent states within the commonwealth, bound solely by their common allegiance to the Crown. However, from a practical point of view, it must be admitted that Canada still lacks certain prerogatives which would ensure her the maturity of a free nation. I now repeat what I said last year: in order to attain the status guaranteed by the Statute of Westminster, our country still lacks three things: first, the right to amend her own constitution; second, a distinctive national flag; third, the abolition of appeals to the privy council. I shall deal only with this third proposal, because it is the one we are discussing today.
We must abolish appeals to the privy council first because our status of sovereign state calls for it; second, we have in Canada all that is required to create a judicial body complete in itself and capable of settling all our disputes; third, present conditions do not lend themselves to the prompt administration of justice for all amenable to law.
First, our status of free nation compels us to abolish appeals to the privy council.
When our country was still a crown colony, it was only logical that the final court of appeal be in the old country. As long as we were not fully autonomous in the matter of legislation, it was only logical that we should not be so in matters of law. But we reached our full constitutional development with the Statute of Westminster. Since then, nothing should prevent our abolishing appeals to a judicial body in another country.
This step has been put off since 1931, when the Statute of Westminster was enacted, and this for reasons of expediency rather than procedure. Inasmuch as last year, the privy council stated the Canadian parliament could, of its own authority, abolish such appeals, there should be no more obstacles to our doing so.
It can be said that since 1931, the country at large has been educated in this matter and public opinion now insists that appeals to the privy council be abolished. It is unworthy of a sovereign state to have its citizens subject in any way whatsoever to court decisions rendered in another state.
We exercise our sovereignty in almost every sphere. In the legislative field, for instance, we are absolutely free to enact whatever laws we choose, and this legislation no outside power can either change or disallow. In matters of international trade, it is entirely up to us to enter into any trade agreement we like, and the same applies to our external policy since we appoint our own ambassadors and diplomatic representatives. In 1939, war was declared by the Canadian parliament and duly accredited Canadian representatives sign peace treaties on Canada's behalf. Why then try to preserve an obsolete link, a state of things that is incompatible with our status of sovereign state?
A sovereign state must control its legislation, manage its external and internal policy and submit to no decisions other than those rendered by tribunals within its own boundaries. That is the main reason why we must do away with appeals to the privy council.
A second reason in support of this bill is the fact that Canada has the required and properly qualified court to pass final judgment on all disputes, whether they relate to the criminal code, the civil code or constitutional law.
In criminal cases, the matter is finalized, and our supreme court has been, for many years, the last tribunal to deal with them. In civil matters, nobody will challenge the fact that our supreme court judges are more conversant with our laws, legislation, jurisprudence, customs and traditions than the lords of the privy council.

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Be it said with due respect to those honourable gentlemen. Why then submit such cases to a British court, if our Canadian court is better able to pass judgment on them?

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Then there are cases of constitutional law, especially litigation relating
Supreme Court Act

to the respective rights and prerogatives of the dominion and provincial governments.
Here it is claimed by advocates by privy council appeals that we should cling to its jurisdiction as a greater protection for the rights of provinces and minorities. To my mind, this claim is groundless. A comparison of supreme court judgments since it was first established with those of the privy council in such matters, will show that the rights of provinces and minorities were no more protected by the privy council than by the supreme court itself. The privy council jurisprudence is like a pendulum which is skillfully made to swing at times in the direction of dominion authority, and at other times toward provincial rights, and it would be quite difficult to ascertain the real trend of that changing jurisprudence.

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPREME -COURT ACT AMENDMENT AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Moreover, to hold that, because they owe their appointment and jurisdiction to the dominion government, the judges would be prejudiced in its favour, would be casting reflections on the impartiality and the quality of our supreme court.
In the United States, the supreme court is called upon to pass final judgments on litigations arising between the states and the federal government. Justices of the United States supreme court are appointed by the central power, yet no one would pretend that their judgments are biased.
I might follow the comparison into another field. It might also be held that our sessions of the peace judges or our district magistrates, in the province of Quebec, are not competent to pass judgment on matters pertaining to federal legislation, because they owe their appointment to the provincial government. Such a statement would be most unfair and ridiculous. If that is so, why challenge the fair-mindedness of our supreme court judges because they were appointed by the dominion government? I believe I need not stress further the weakness of such an argument.
But even if we were to admit that assertion for the sake of the discussion, it does not follow that we should submit litigations of a constitutional nature to the judgment of a court which is not our own. All we have to do, if necessary, is to amend our judicial system, but I cannot agree that a sovereign federal state is unable to settle its own constitutional . Or judicial problems, that it must submit them to the court of another country.

Lastly, there is a practical problem which we cannot ignore when dealing with the question of abolishing appeals to the privy council. Justice in this democratic country must be prompt and, as far as possible, within the reach of all who come under it. Now, when a case is to go to the privy council, it necessarily takes a long time before the matter is submitted to the final authority. In the province of Quebec, the case is tried first by the superior court, then by the court of king's bench sitting on appeal. Then another appeal is lodged with the supreme court sitting in Ottawa and, at long last, the case is taken to the privy council.
How about the high cost of canwing a case to the privy council? Men of wealth and power can manage it rather easily but those of small means, who cannot meet the cost, often prefer to drop the case or settle out of court on more or less satisfactory terms. To such may be applied the famous lines of fabulist de La Fontaine:
According as to whether thou art mighty or penniless
Court judgments shall make thee white or black.
I do not wish to labour the point. Mr. Speaker, but I do think I have made it sufficiently clear that appeals to the privy council are unworthy of a sovereign state, that they do not conform to our present status, that we have here in our own country, courts of law which are perfectly competent to pass judgment on all our cases, and that such a tribunal-i.e. the privy council-does not suit the needs of those who require the expeditious justice within the means of all.
For these reasons I support the bill before us at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to this bill, because last year I was opposed to the principle of a similar bill. As the house knows, there are two classes of appeals involved in appeals to the privy council. One class relates to statutory appeals from the dominion or the provinces, the other class to appeals as a matter of grace, which no legislature in the empire can change. It is the right of any British subject to petition His Majesty in his privy council. I have here the very learned opinion of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, who was not only one of the most honoured members of the legal profession but chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, and at other times solicitor general, minister of justice, and afterwards lieutenant governor of a great province of this dominion. In an

Supply-Justice
address to the Canadian Bar Association in 1914, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick gave his opinion on appeals to the privy council. He said:
In no part of the king's dominions has greater service been rendered by the judicial committee than in Canada, particularly since confederation.
Since 1867, the judicial committee has been called upon in scores of cases to trace out the line of demarcation between federal and provincial jurisdiction, and it must be truthfully said that the result has been eminently satisfactory. Removed, as the majority of judges are, from all local strifes, desirous as they are to distribute the most impartial justice, it is not surprising that the right of appeal to the king in his privy council is one of the privileges most highly prized by the people of the dominion. I do not mean to say that there has not been exception taken to the freedom with which appeals may be carried to the privy council in ordinary civil matters, but whatever view may obtain in other parts of the empire, so far as Canada is concerned, I think I may safely say that, amongst lawyers and judges competent to speak on the subject, there is but one opinion, that where constitutional questions are concerned an appeal to the judicial committee must always be retained.
I am offering that opinion to balance to some extent the opposite opinions which have been offered. I rather think the judicial committee of the privy council has rendered a real service to Canada. Their decisions have been one judgment, no dissenting judgments.
Mr. Conant, when attorney general of Ontario, gave opinions which almost coincide with those of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. I quote:
Yesterday Attorney General Conant redirected public attention to one of the most contentious questions with which the forthcoming session of parliament will have to deal. It is the age-old proposal to abolish appeals to the privy council, formally introduced at the last session by Hon. C. H. Cahan. Then, as always, opinion was found to be strongly divided, and the bill was held over when the minister of justice suggested that it was too important a matter for summary decision.
_ It is important, vitally important, to the future of Canada and the commonwealth, and the considered opinion of Ontario's attorney general should be a valuable guide to the House of Commons debate. His opinion is based on both domestic and imperial considerations, none of which can or should be left out of unbiased deliberations. "With greatest respect for this (the appeal court) and all other Canadian courts," he said. "I incline to the view that in matters and cases involving constitutional questions, particularly in issues between the dominion and a province or between provinces, the right of appeal to the privy council should be continued."
This, emphatically, is not the view of some who are perhaps, quite as competent to judge. It is not the view of the sponsor of the bill. Whatever Mr. Cahan may think, there are many experts who cannot share his judgment.
In addition we have the opinion of probably the greatest lawyer which this country ever
produced, namely, Sir Allen Aylesworth. I remember going into the court of appeal and seeing him handling the whole docket by himself. Three or four years ago Sir Allen Aylesworth said:
Now, when it becomes at least an academic question, if not a practical one, whether this parliament should do anything to limit or cut down that right of appeal, I desire to question, and to question strongly, the competence of any Canadian parliament to do anything of the sort. Of course, no one would argue that a mere resolution of one house of parliament would have any such effect.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister something about the prosecution of the dental corporations and what has been done in consequence of the direction of Mr. Justice Barlow to the jury that the evidence which was submitted by the crown was of such a nature that their verdict should be one of not guilty. I brought this matter up at the time the case was tried; for I found it very difficult to understand, having regard to the direct statements made in the volume issued by the commissioner of combines, that the judge under the circumstances should find that there was no evidence.
As I remember it, for I have not the notes before me, the judge directed the jury to bring in an acquittal because of the failure of the prosecution to make out a ease: first, because of failure to prorre that the documents which were taken from the possession of the
Supply-Justice

nineteen defendants were in fact documents signed by the representatives of those defendants; and, secondly, because of the failure of the prosecution to prove that these companies were in fact incorporated companies and that the individuals in question, who had signed the letters upon which the prosecutions were based, were in fact officials of the corporations.
The answer given by the minister at the time was that the course followed by the prosecution in failing to prove these obvious matters was an intentional course. Well, if that be so, I should like the minister to explain this. If it was an intentional course, why did the crown counsel, upon the judge indicating the position he would take in regard to the prosecution, and the direction he would give to the jury, then ask for leave to introduce further evidence, which would be admissible, under the rules of court, only provided that the failure to prove these necessary elements was the result of inadvertence or mistake? That is the first question I raise in regard to the combines investigation branch.
The second question I will now state. I can quite realize that one of the arguments which might be advanced for the publication of reports on the part of the commissioner investigating combines is that publicity is a valuable deterrent. But I return to the matter which I dealt with the other day, or to which at any rate, I casually referred. Is there any justification for trying an individual by reports from government departments, before the bar of public opinion, which reports indicate the guilt of those mentioned, when subsequently prosecutions may take place?
I have no sympathy for those who exploit. Indeed, the minister will remember that it was an amendment which I suggested two years ago, accepted by his predecessor in office, that restored to private individuals anywhere in this country the right to take proceedings against combines designed to exploit the public. On the other hand. I think fairness demands that when an official such as the commissioner in charge of the Combines Investigation Act makes an examination of individuals allegedly guilty of infractions of the act, the conclusions at which he has arrived, as a result of the questions asked the individuals involved, or following investigation in general, should not be embodied in a public report until after prosecution has taken place.
I am not in any way considering at the moment the merits of the case against the optical companies. I have no interest in them either directly or indirectly, nor indeed has any one of them communicated with me. But I have an abiding sense of what is fair, and

I believe the people as a whole have the same sense. I do not think it can be justified that individuals shall be found, as it were, guilty, by public authority in a public document, until the courts determine the question in the affirmative.
I should like to hear from the minister on these two questions, both of which I consider important.
We have had a committee sitting on prices for the past four months, and I suppose, as well, the commissioner has been investigating alleged profiteering in this country. What has been done by him in that connection? How many members has he on his staff investigating profiteering? To what degree has consideration been given to prosecutions, and how many prosecutions have in fact taken place against alleged profiteers who are exploiting the public?
A statement from the minister on the general set-up of the combines investigation branch today would be timely, for I remember the former minister of justice stating two years ago that up to that time there were no teeth in the legislation nor was there a sufficient force to act with dispatch, but that with the amendments, a new era would have dawned and action would be the result wherever wrongdoing was ascertained.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman has asked1 me two or three questions in connection with the administration of the Combines Investigation Act. The first question related to the prosecution of the alleged dental combine.
As the committee knows, proceedings against members of the Canadian dental trade association were instituted on the direction of the Attorney General of Canada, on indictment by a grand jury. Eighteen corporate members of the association were charged with offences against section 498 of the criminal code and tried before Mr. Justice F. H. Barlow of the Supreme Court of Ontario sitting with a jury. The trial began on February 23. 1948, and ended on March 18, 1948, when the judge directed the jury to return a verdict of not guilty on the ground that the evidence submitted by the crown had not been adequately authenticated.
The crown is appealing from this decision and the Ontario Court of Appeal has decided to hear the appeal in September. Now, since the ease is on appeal, it would hardly be appropriate for me to argue the points of law, even if I were briefed, as I am not. But my understanding is that counsel for the prosecution gave consideration to this question as to whether it was necessary to prove the

Supply-Justice
authority of those who signed these documents to act for the defendants, the companies, and relying on certain cases he decided it was not necessary. I presume it would have been an enormous job. The case took a long time as it was. Whether that had anything to do with it or not, I do not know. It is true that, after a long argument, counsel for the crown did make application at the last moment to be allowed to call evidence to prove that those who signed the documents did so on behalf of the defendants in the action. That application was denied. My hon. friend asks me, if it was not inadvertence, why that application was made. I am not in a position to answer that, but I think I- have been in cases myself where at a late date I decided that, in view of the reaction of the presiding judge or something of the kind, perhaps I had better do something I had not planned to do at the outset of the case.
But not after your case was closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. At any rate that is a matter which I cannot answer. Mr. D. L. McCarthy was senior counsel and Mr. Peter Wright was junior counsel; there was a large number of counsel. But Mr. McCarthy had a great deal of experience. All we can do is to get the best counsel we can, place the case in their hands and be guided by their advice. As I say, the case is on appeal.
The second question the hon. gentleman asked me is an important and interesting one; that is, whether this act is fair in the provision that it makes. It must be borne in mind that we are on the estimates here tonight, and I do not know whether we should1 be considering the principle of the Combines Investigation Act. The act is not before the house for amendment. The relevant sections are first, section 12, which reads as follows:
The commissioner shall, on application made under section 11 of this act, or whenever he has reason to believe that a combine exists or is being formed, or on direction by the minister, cause an inquiry to be made into all such matters as he considers necessary to inquire into with the view of determining whether a combine exists or is being formed.
And then later, section 27, paragraph 5, is to this effect;
Any report of the commissioner or of a special commissioner, other than an interim report or a report of a preliminary inquiry under section 13 of this act, shall within fifteen days after its receipt by the minister be made public unless the commissioner states in writing to the minister that he believes the public interest would be better served by withholding publication, in which case the minister may decide whether the report, either in whole or in part, shall be made public.
As I said the other day when the hon. member raised this question on the orders of the day, that section or a similar section has been in the act from 1910 down to the present time. Of course, from 1923 until 1935, I think, the registrar was the important man; the general course was that the registrar made an investigation and a report, and the act was silent as to whether that report should be published or not. But if he reported that there was a prima facie evidence of a combine, a special commissioner was appointed ; and the special commissioner's report was subject to exactly these provisions. From 1937 on, those provisions have been in the act.
I submit that it is necessary that there be publicity. At least, it is my contention or submission that there should be publicity. This offence is not at all like an offence that speaks for itself. It is all a mystery. The public has no way of knowing whether there is any combine or not. It is not like theft, bank robbery or any of those other overt or open acts where it is clear that there has been an offence. Here there is just a dark surmise and that is all. If the public is to know anything at all about this, it must be explained to them by the report of somebody who has made an investigation. If you have no provision that that report is to be made public, there is no possibility of an opportunity for public opinion to operate on governments, attorneys general or ministers of justice. There is no possibility of that; and you have to make a strong assumption that public officials will be fully alive to their responsibilities.
My hon. friend is not fond of delegating these great responsibilities to the ministers of the crown. I know that from what he has said in the house. In a matter of this kind I think the operation of public opinion is something to be encouraged. That does not mean that the commissioner should put in anything he feels like putting in that report. It does not mean that he should build up a brief there for the prosecution. It does not mean that he should seek to influence public opinion in a one-sided way. I think it is open to argument that there ought to be some safeguards of what is the purpose in the report. But after all, there is not much difference between the publication of a report by the commissioner and a preliminary inquiry into a criminal action. The commissioner has no judicial power; that is, he cannot himself determine the guilt of the accused. All he can do is express an
Supply-Justice

opinion. The question is how far he should go in expressing an opinion, and whether he should not confine himself fairly well to facts.
I agree with my hon. friend that that matter is open to argument, as to how far the commissioner should go in that report. But I think there must be a report, and that as soon as he makes it, it should be made public in the normal case. I thoroughly understand the difficulty that my hon. friend points out. It is not usually done. It is done in a preliminary inquiry. People everywhere read all the evidence against the accused. They read that he is committed for trial, and that there is a prima facie case against him. Yet that is not deemed to be contrary to the principles of ratural justice and to be poisoning the minds of the public against the accused, because they understand that it is to be followed by a trial, that then they will hear the other side, and that there may be another side. The trial is deemed to be a fair one. So long as it is understood that this is the result of an inquiry which necessarily precedes a trial, and so long as restraint is exercised by the commissioner in making a report, I doubt whether there is any serious infringement of the principle of natural justice.

Mr. Chairman, the recent increase in salaries has been very much appreciated by the force as a whole, and was a step in the right direction. At the present moment I am not going to advocate any further increases, although I believe that at a very early day, certainly within the next few months, consideration will have to be given to further increases in certain specific ranks within the R.C.M.P.
I have a number of questions to ask in this connection. I would ask, first, the degree to which the mounted police is being maintained at strength. During the war their work on behalf of the war effort was effective and magnificent. Since the war they have been engaged in the enforcement of law, in the enforcement of dominion statutes and they have also been used in various municipalities as a municipal force.
On the last occasion the estimates were discussed I brought up the question as to whether sufficient recruits were being secured to meet the wastages apparent immediately following the war, when quite a large number of trained men ceased to serve at the conclusion of their period of service, and did not seek re-enlistment. The answer I then received was that sufficient men were available. Recently a campaign was started, and it still continues, to secure recruits, such applicants to be single, and between the ages of eighteen and thirty years. I should like to know the degree to which this campaign has been successful.
The second point I wish to raise has to do with investigation into the activities of communism in this country. On many occasions mention has been made of the report of the royal commission. In that report a significant finding was made, namely, that there exists in Canada a fifth column organized and directed by Russian agents in Canada and in Russia.
The second finding as it appears at page 685 of the report states:
Within the fifth column there are several spy rings.

The next finding was:
We have been able to identify many of the members of one of these rings, namely, that of which Colonel Zabotin was the head in Canada. . . . Without documents such as Gouzenko placed before us we cannot identify any nonRussian members of the other rings.
What evidence is there or was there to support that finding? What evidence is there now that there exists in Canada a number of rings designed to undermine the state from within? That was a finding definite in its effect. The royal commission acted only in respect of one of these rings. I am asking the minister to let the Canadian people know what I asked him to let them know recently, at which time he replied that when the mounted police estimates came up the matter could be discussed. I am asking him to give to the people of this country some idea of the degree to which various organizations under Russian domination are in fac-t operating today in this country to the detriment of the country, and designed to sabotage our system and our form of government.
The finding is made by the commission. I ask the minister, without disclosing in detail matters which might be necessary to keep within the confines of the reports of the mounted police, the degree to which there was reason -for this finding, and some indication of the amplitude of the government operating under communistic auspices.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it would be in the public interest to discuss fully the knowledge the police have.
Just the general indications.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I must say I have not that knowledge myself. I could not give it to the committee. I could- .get it, I presume, by going into the matter carefully with the police. But to talk about these rings, how far they have been pursued, where they are and what they are, would not be a proper thing to do.
I could not hear the last of what the minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I just said what I said at the outset, that it would be improper, I believe, for me to give information in the House of Commons of Canada to the public about police activities and the detecting of communistic activities, where it is going on, what is going on, who is doing it, and so on.

Oh, Mr. Chairman, no one ever suggested that, and I made that clear. A finding has been made by a commission that there are several spy rings operating

in this country, and I am asking the minister whether or not such spy rings are operating.
I am not asking anything about the proceedings that are being taken by the R.C.M.P., but I want to know and I think the Canadian people have a right to know whether there is a spy ring or several spy rings operating here according to a finding made by a royal commission. I am not asking for any particulars of the investigation that may be going on. I had something to do with prosecutions in connection with this very matter long years ago, and I know something of the reports made by the mounted police and their activities. I think the Canadian people have a right to be apprised whether or not such rings in fact exist.

Last week there came into my hands a periodical sent out by someone connected with the R.C.M.P. During the war, applications were made to the mounted police by

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Rightly or wrongly, I have taken the position that it is not the business of the R.C.M.P. to act as a reservoir for municipal police. The R.C.M.P. needs certain reserves; they have peaks of demand and so forth, and therefore it is desirable that the R.C.M.P. should do some municipal policing, but not all that is asked of them, because this policing is being supplied at about half its cost to the municipalities, and the R.C.M.P. should not be maintained as a sort of source of subsidized policing for municipalities. For that reason we have never felt that we were under an obligation to load up our force with policemen to be used by towns wherever they wanted them; but, as I say, some towns are being policed. That is desirable in the interests of the force itself because, while they are operating as municipal police, they are available in an emergency for federal service. But it is a federal force, and the policy should be based upon federal requirements, including the requirements of policing the provinces, which is done by agreement with the provinces.

One matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee is the pay of tradesmen attached to the R.C.M.P., not in the force personnel, but the administrative branch. I wonder if the minister or the officials in front of him are sufficiently
