familiar with the ease of Doctor E. A. Braith-waite of Edmonton for me to ask a question or two and in particular for the minister to make a comment. As I assume the minister knows, from the way he nodded his head, Doctor Braithwaite is now eighty-six years of age. His connection with the mounted police extended over a good many years. I am told that his total service in the Northwest Mounted Police, the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police amounted to forty-seven years and eight months, beginning away back in 1884. Of that period I understand that some twenty-eight years were spent in the ranks and as an honorary surgeon of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The problem of Doctor Braithwaite is that of a pension. I understand that the matter has been taken up with the officers of the department a good many times by a good many friends who have been interested in this case. Doctor Braithwaite feels that he has claim to a pension; and many of those who know him and know of the long service he rendered to the force are surprised that he is not in receipt of a pension. However, I must be realistic in discussing this matter and admit that the minister has pointed out to me by letter that in his view Doctor Braithwaite does not have a legal claim to a pension. Nevertheless, I judge from a letter the minister wrote me on June 19, 1947, that the department has recognized a considerable moral claim on the part of Doctor Braithwaite, and considerable merit in the claim he has put forward. I base that statement on the fact that apparently the matter has gone to treasury board on at least one occasion, with the suggestion that a special vote by parliament might be asked, or even a special act passed.
If the Department of Justice has made a request of that kind to treasury board it would seem to indicate, I say, that there is merit in Doctor Braithwaite's claim for some kind of pension. In the letter to which I referred, the minister said treasury board had turned down this request, at least when it was made by one of his predecessors. I wonder whether a further request has been made to treasury board. If not, in view of the continued representations by Doctor Braithwaite and his friends, I wonder whether the minister would look into the matter further and see if something cannot be done for this man who gave so much service to the mounted police and who is now such an honoured elder citizen of the province of Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, this case has been up quite often. My hon. friend
fMr. Knowles.]
says there is a presumption that if a request was made it was justified. I do not know that there is any such presumption. The presumption might be that treasury board was right about it rather than the minister who made the request. I do not know; I do not think I have made a request since I have been in the department. There has been a difference of opinion in the service, perhaps, about this case; but one thing is sure, and that is that there is no legal claim to pension. I am informed that this gentleman was a part-time doctor for a long time; that he never contributed to any pension fund; that he is not pensionable, and that it is just a question whether it is desirable to vote him a pension. It is not a legal question at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I ask the minister whether he has looked into the case since he has taken over this department? I realize that he must have a great many matters to which he must attend personally; but the correspondence I have had concerning this case makes me feel that it would merit the personal attention of the minister. There does seem to be some dispute as to the kind of connection he had with the force. Certainly the doctor is of the opinion that he was in the force in every possible way. The minister tells me the doctor did not have a commission from the crown and therefore, he does not have the kind of claim he puts forth. On the other hand, let me quote from the minister's letter to me, to which I have already referred:
As Doctor Braithwaite was an honorary surgeon in the force, and still is, he was awarded the long service medal in 1928 in recognition of his long connection with the force.
The very fact that this matter has been considered to such an extent, and that a former minister of justice sent it to treasury board does, I submit, establish some presumption as to the moral and humanitarian claim, at any rate, of this old gentleman. So I hope the ease may yet be given the kind of personal attention that seems to be necessary if anything is to be done for him.

As a former chairman of the Toronto police commission I have seen something of the good work done by the mounted police. They carried on through a long war, when they were enforcing tens of thousands of orders in council; and this is a very small amount of money to provide for those who have been injured while on duty. Following every war, as you know, there is a great deal of disorder throughout the country. As a result, these officers have to go out by night and by day and meet desperadoes and

Supply-R.C.M.P.
all kinds of people on the street; and they may lose their lives. Here we are voting only $13,000 to compensate members of this force for injuries received in- the discharge of their duties. That is a very small amount, and I can tell you that the sum required in our city, where there are over a thousand policemen, is much larger. I understand that provision is being made for the future, in many cases by an insurance, scheme which recently passed the house, but I urge that there should be increases, not only in this item but in those dealing with the pensions paid to the dependents of those members of the force who gave their lives in the discharge of their duty. Peace has its heroes as well as war, and we would not consider giving such a small pension as is provided in the next item to a soldier injured in battle.
I want to commend the minister for the improvement he has made in his department. He has been hard working, conscientious and moderate in what he asks; but I urge that there should be a better deal for all ranks of the mounted police. On many occasions they have come to the support of the civil authorities, and they are doing excellent work. If you want to get good men for the force from now on you will have to increase the provision to look after them when they are injured, and to look after their wives and children if they should be killed.

I listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre speak of a very old friend of mine, Doctor Braithwaite. Perhaps I can agree with the hon. member, in the event we want to pension everybody, whether they contribute toward that pension or not. I know Doctor Braithwaite very well. He was with the mounted police, and now he is the chief coroner. I will go back a year; he may have died in the meantime. But up to a year ago he was chief coroner in the province of Alberta.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He is definitely alive. I had a letter from him less than a week ago.
Frankly, I think he is infinitely more alive than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. But, still, that is merely my opinion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Probably right.
It is neither here nor there.
That is a presumption.

Let us not talk about presumption. I know the doctor very well, and he has not done badly. It is a very rude expression, I know, but a great 5849-313
many people in Canada who have been feeding out of the public trough have not done badly. And now we, great fellows, all say that they must have pensions.
I am one of those people who do not believe in that. Certainly, with respect to our ill, our incompetent and our crippled, I believe in that sort of thing. I do not know this, but I am inclined to think that if we do not give Doctor Braithwaite a pension under the mounted police estimates the dear old fellow will not suffer very much.
But I know the socialists! They think everybody should have a pension. As a matter of fact, I imagine tomorrow they will introduce into the house in some manner or another, under some subterfuge, a suggestion as to a pension for the two people who have been recently elected to parliament-and I congratulate them upon that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Thank you.
And my guess is that tonight in Vancouver Centre they will have another fellow. And so they will have a special bill-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He is leading at the halfway mark.
You must be wrong about that. After all, I know something about time zones in this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I was quoting a Canadian Press report.

The Canadian Press says he is leading at the half-way mark?
I will go farther with you: He will be elected. That is my judgment. I was there, you see. I do not think there is any doubt about it, that he will be elected in Vancouver Centre. And, having met the gentleman, when he comes here with you delightful gentlemen I say you have a problem on your hands; because he is a radical, to the extent of being a communist. So now, all that you have sown will be reaped within your own party. You will have difficulty with that young man.
He will be a bigger problem to you fellows.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On a point of order, I have absolutely no objection to the hon. member for Calgary West making his political remarks at the proper time. But I do object to this sort of thing being dragged in, in connection with the case of this old gentleman, Doctor Braithwaite. Surely it is clear that I am not appealing for votes in the city of Edmonton; there is no by-election on there, and Doctor Braithwaite is only one old gentleman, eight-six years of age. I have raised this
Supply-R .C.M.P.

case with some reluctance. I have had some correspondence with him for several years, but until now I have not raised the matter on the floor of the house.
I am surprised he ever wrote to you. But go on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Progress has been too slow. Hence I raised the matter tonight in all earnestness and in good faith, and I am sorry the hon. member for Calgary West has used the terms he has in connection with this case. He can say all these things about me or about the party any time he wishes, when we have a field day on that sort of thing. It is sheer nonsense, but we shall be glad to deal with it at the proper time. But we are now discussing an item respecting pensions for members of the mounted police force, and I suggest that the hon. member for Calgary West get back to that phase of the matter and give us a hand in this plea for Doctor Braithwaite.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, let me agree with everything my very good friend has said. But he will probably remember that I was turned aside twice because of interruptions from persons who sit behind him. I agree that we should stay within the rails; and if he would but control his own irrepressible youth who are sitting behind him, then of course I would have stayed within the rails and gone along with the discussion as we have had it.
Now that he tells me that he is a great pal of my friend Doctor Braithwaite, who is eighty-six years of age, I am inclined to think he should be very proud that my very good friend Doctor Braithwaite wrote him a letter at all. That is the greatest compliment I can pay to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, because, after all, the doctor is an old gentleman.
Hear, hear.

I am certainly glad to hear that. I have been with him on many inquests. The doctor is not a lawyer. He has been our chief coroner; and if he could take care of some of the cadavers who are immediately to my left he could come to some excellent conclusions, which I think would do great credit to the doctor and to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Have I
apologized to you sufficiently?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Quite.

Then that is fine. I am so happy to have the hon. 
member for Winnipeg North Centre agree with me; because, of all the people in the House of Commons, of all the members I have seen in the house in the short time I have been here, he is the most generous with other people's money. I am very fond of him. I like his wit. At times it is incisive and, at other times, it is difficult to find. And when I meet him in the corridor and he explains his smart remarks to me, dumb as I am, after plenty of explanation, I finally find out exactly what he means-or perhaps the word "exactly" is badly used. Perhaps I should say I get a glimmering of the idea he had in his head before he destroyed it by talking. So we are getting along beautifully.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Beautifully!

At the
present time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And we are all enjoying it.

"Enjoying it"?-that word "enjoying" is a wonderful word. I have enjoyed what has happened in the last few days. I enjoy punishment, if it is delicate; but I admit I am not very happy about it-about what has happened in the last few days. I will not say I enjoyed it, because I can see the future. I will admit I am not happy.
But may I congratulate my very good friend upon his being so happy because of joining with the communists. They are now the big shots in politics in this country.
Oh, oh.
I am trying to-*
Very nicely put.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But completely false.
As he knows.

"Very nicely put"; "but completely false". The fellow who said, "as he knows" is, of course, just a partisan who will say anything. There is no truth in what he said. "Very nicely put"-I accept that. And somebody else says, "Completely false"-I do not mind that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You accept that, too.

I do not mind anyone saying that what I have said is completely false. That is a matter of opinion, so I cannot object to the statement by the hon. member for Regina City. You see, he has not been there very long. I was born there, and I know all about that place. I know about the decent pioneers who made

Supply-R.C.M.P.
that part of the country. So now we are in the position, because people have children-
You are not the only pioneer there, either.

No, I am not the only pioneer. My people came up in 1882, ahead of the railway, which got through in February of 1883. I was born only in 1886. The hon. member for Regina City is a great friend of my older brother and has been trying to beat him at golf, for the last fifty years. He has failed in that as in anything else against the Smith family.
To come back to my very good friend, Doctor Braithwaite, I will not oppose any pension to Doctor Braithwaite whether he needs it or not. Is that a fair answer to what my hon. friend has said? The only reason he said this is to show how he is looking after our old people, but Doctor Braithwaite does not need looking after. But let me join my hon. friend in the broad position that we must look after our old people. I shall be delighted if Doctor Braithwaite gets $2.50, or $250, or $2,500. That would be nothing to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, as I remember so well.
And by-elections.

I had forgotten about that election back there. I remember so well that in New York there was once a man named Gates. He was quite busy in the stock market, and in the early days when railroads were being built he became known as "Bet You A Million Gates." I have often wondered what dire circumstances would ensue if "Bet You A Million Gates" had ever met "What's a Million Howe."

I have been trying to brush up on the correspondence mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but I have not had time to digest all of it. I should like to repeat what has been so well said to the minister by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. If there is any way by which this technicality could be overcome, I appeal to the minister to take the appropriate action.
This old gentleman has a long record of distinguished service, I believe going back as far as 1885. He is a friend of mine, because I worked with him in the government of Alberta for a number of years. A better chief coroner I have never seen anywhere. He used to tell me about his experiences while he was with the R.C.M.P. The minister has pointed out quite rightly that he was an honorary surgeon, but in whatever capacity he may have 5849-3134
served, I am sure that he did it to the best of his ability, and his ability was great. If there is any way by which this technicality can be removed and Doctor Braithwaite given some consideration I would be happy to see it done.
Is it a matter of general policy of the department to grant pensions to the R.C.M.P.?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We discussed a pension system in the bill which I had before the house earlier this session and which instituted a new pension system. There have been pension systems in the past, but this gentleman did not come under any of them. He has made no contribution. For a long period of time he was a part-time doctor-
An honorary surgeon.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -with the R.C.M.P., and he continued to carry on his private practice. There was a time back in the days of the Riel rebellion when he was in the R.C.M.P. as a surgeon but not long enough to qualify for a pension.

I remember the contributory pensions provided for by the bill referred to by the minister. I was just wondering where all this reference to by-elections, communists and so forth came into the picture. I think we are wasting a lot of time. If a member of the R.C.M.P. served in the years before there was a pension scheme and did not have an opportunity of contributing, then I think there should be some administrative latitude to take care of extenuating circumstances. If a scheme had not been inaugurated at that time, that was not the fault of the service; it was the fault of those who administered the act.
This is not something peculiar to the R.C.M.P. We find it in many other industries across the country. Doctor Braithwaite was one of the pioneers in this service, and in our industrial set-up there are many old pioneers who are receiving no pensions and who are being relegated to the streets. They cannot come under the pension schemes that are being established.
The hon. member for Calgary West has assured us that this particular gentleman will suffer no hardship, but there may be other cases where hardships exist. I think, where anyone has made a contribution, as this gentleman has, to his country in tt: past and will in the future, the Department of Justice should be able to look after him in the event of circumstances arising over which he has no control and which cause extreme hardship.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It occurred to me that some of the items might be non-controversial. Ordinarily the penitentiary item takes a long time, and I would prefer not to consider it tonight.

I should like to say a few words about the question of crime comics. What I have to say will not take so very long, but I want to ask the minister a number of questions. If he prefers to leave this item until tomorrow it will be acceptable to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the questions are relevant to the item I think the hon. member had better ask them, so that I can read them in Hansard in the morning and perhaps be in a better position to answer.

I brought this matter up under the general item, so that I might suggest to the minister certain measures to combat the increasing number of crimes by juveniles and to halt the increase of juvenile delinquency. Recently I have had brought to my attention a number of so-called crime comics which are widely circulated throughout Canada. This fact, coupled with the evidence of increasing juvenile delinquency, seems to me to demand that this House of Commons should request the minister to take certain steps to lessen the tendencies and to combat the causes. This is one of the active causes of juvenile delinquency. Unfortunately I have not yet got an answer to the question I put on the order paper asking how many offences under the criminal code, which might be classed as crimes of violence, have been committed by offenders eighteen years and under in each of the years 1946, 1947 and 1948. The minister will remember that quite a number of shocking crimes have been committed by juveniles in recent months. One of the most shocking was in Montreal recently, where a boy twelve years of age beat his mother to death with a baseball bat. He simply found her sleeping, lying there defenceless, picked up a bat and beat in her head for no apparent reason, except that, when being tried, he said he had seen that sort of thing in the comics.
This question has also been raised by the council of women who met recently in Ottawa. I have not seen all their resolutions, but I have been in discussion with some of the members of the council from my own part of the country and they said this question was vexing their minds to a great extent.

I have no official figures on the circulation of these magazines, but an estimate made by a responsible authority in Kamloops, a city of only 12,000 people, is that 15,000 of these magazines are sold on the newsstands there every month. They are sold as an article for profit. They are, I will not say attractively, but gaudily got up, so that they appeal to juveniles by their colours as they lie on the magazine racks. As if that were not bad enough, I have studied three of these magazines recently. I have one in my hand, "Green Hornet Fights Crime". Others I have seen, under a general title, which go on to say, "Crime Does Not Pay". That is the sort of cynical approach they make on the front cover. They are printed in Canada. The one I have in my hand is published bi-monthly in Toronto; Lou Ruby, publisher. It goes on to say "Second-class mailing rates approved by post office, Toronto. Any similarity between the characters contained in the comic section and any person either living or dead is coincidental. Printed in Canada by the Globe Printing Company, Toronto." This magazine sells on the newsstands for ten cents a copy.
I have spoken to people who have had experience in this type of thing and in dealing with juvenile delinquents in magistrates courts and so on, and they say that, without any doubt, this type of magazine is printed in a form which is calculated to make the maximum impression on juvenile minds. They portray crimes of violence, in pictures, with a few words as a caption which are easily understood.
I just want to give an example from the one I have in my hand. It starts off on the inside cover with the picture of a man striking a match and staring at it. The caption over the next picture is, "Tonight I dreamed of a blazing moon like a fiery wheel in the sky-burning trees were crashing about me," and the caption is illustrated. The next picture portrays him walking to a slum tenement, and he says, "I saw an old condemned building. Nobody would care if it burned down." The next picture shows this man holding a burning match, and the caption says, "Tonight I stole into the cellar of the condemned building and set my first fire." That is a fine thing to put before a youngster of twelve or so, who perhaps has just struck his first match.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, he would strike it before that.

The minister says, "Oh". Is he shaking his head in disagreement? As I say, it is difficult to prove that these magazines do actually increase juvenile delinquency, but one can say at least that two coincidences

Supply-R.C.MP.
go together, that there is an increase in juvenile delinquency and an increase in the circulation of this type of magazine in Canada.
I want to suggest certain specific remedies which might be taken to prevent the circulation of this type of magazine. The first one is direct censorship. I know the answer to that may be that since this comes under the heading of property and civil rights, it falls under provincial jurisdiction, and I suppose that to some extent that argument must be conceded to be valid. But certainly, in so far as the federal Department of Justice has any jurisdiction, it can, I think, directly order that the publication of these magazines be banned in Canada and, is so far as it has federal jurisdiction, prosecute anyone who publishes such magazines. Questions of the freedom of the press do not, I think, enter, because freedom has never yet meant license, and this type of thing is not freedom but license. It is abusing liberty to make a profit practically out of the advocacy of crime.
